T1001.description: Obfuscates command and control traffic content, without necessarily encrypting it, using junk data, steganography or protocol impersonation so commands are harder to detect or decipher.

T1001.001.description: Inserts random or meaningless junk bytes into C2 protocol traffic, by prepending, appending or interleaving characters, to defeat trivial decoding and signature-based analysis.

T1001.002.description: Hides command and control data inside images, documents or other digital files exchanged between systems, using steganographic embedding so C2 messages appear as benign media.

T1001.003.description: Disguises C2 traffic as legitimate protocols or web services by faking SSL/TLS handshakes or crafting HTTP headers, URIs and certificates that mimic trusted services like Gmail or Google Drive.

T1003.description: Dumps account credentials such as password hashes or cleartext passwords from operating system caches, memory or credential stores for reuse in lateral movement.

T1003.001.description: Reads or dumps LSASS process memory via procdump, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, mimikatz or silent process exit, or registers malicious SSP DLLs, to harvest logged-on users' hashes, tickets and plaintext passwords.

T1003.002.description: Extracts local account password hashes from the Security Account Manager database, via in-memory tools or saving HKLM\SAM and SYSTEM registry hives for offline parsing.

T1003.003.description: Copies the Active Directory database NTDS.dit from a domain controller or backups, using ntdsutil, volume shadow copies or Invoke-NinjaCopy, to extract all domain account hashes.

T1003.004.description: Extracts LSA secrets such as service account credentials from HKLM\SECURITY\Policy\Secrets via registry export or memory using SYSTEM privileges and tools like mimikatz.

T1003.005.description: Extracts cached domain logon hashes (DCC2/MS-Cache v2 on Windows, SSSD or Quest caches on Linux) stored for offline authentication, requiring cracking since they cannot be passed.

T1003.006.description: Impersonate a domain controller via the directory replication API (DRSUAPI GetNCChanges) to remotely pull password hashes, including KRBTGT, from Active Directory without touching NTDS.dit on disk.

T1003.007.description: Read Linux process memory through /proc/<PID>/maps and /proc/<PID>/mem, scanning with regex patterns for cleartext credentials or cached hashes held by running processes.

T1003.008.description: Read or copy Linux /etc/passwd and /etc/shadow, often merging them with unshadow, to obtain password hashes for offline cracking.

T1005.description: Search and gather files, configs, local databases, VM files or process memory from the compromised host's own storage prior to exfiltration, distinct from network shares or removable media.

T1006.description: Open logical volumes or raw disk handles directly and parse file system structures to read or write files, bypassing Windows file ACLs, locks and file system monitoring.

T1007.description: Enumerate registered local system services and scheduled tasks using utilities like sc query, tasklist /svc, net start or systemctl to shape follow-on actions.

T1008.description: Switch to backup or alternate command-and-control channels, servers or protocols when the primary channel is blocked or unavailable to keep reliable communication.

T1010.description: List open application windows and their titles via native APIs or scripts to learn system usage, spot data worth collecting, or identify security tools.

T1011.description: Exfiltrate data over a different physical network medium than the C2 channel, such as WiFi, cellular modem or RF, bypassing enterprise network defenses.

T1011.001.description: Exfiltrate data over a Bluetooth link instead of the wired C2 channel, requiring physical proximity and avoiding monitored enterprise network paths.

T1012.description: Query Windows Registry keys and values with reg.exe or registry APIs to learn OS configuration, installed software and security settings that shape follow-on actions.

T1014.description: Hide processes, files, network connections, drivers or services by hooking and modifying OS API calls at user, kernel, hypervisor or firmware level.

T1016.description: Enumerate local network configuration such as IP and MAC addresses, interfaces, routes and ARP tables via OS utilities, network device CLI or esxcli.

T1016.001.description: Check whether a compromised host can reach the Internet via ping, tracert, web GET requests or speed tests before contacting C2, also revealing proxies and routes.

T1016.002.description: Collect saved or nearby Wi-Fi network names and passwords using netsh wlan, wlanapi.dll calls, NetworkManager connection files or macOS keychain queries.

T1018.description: List other hosts on the network by IP or hostname using net view, ping sweeps, hosts files, ARP cache or network device CLI to identify lateral movement targets.

T1020.description: Exfiltrate collected data automatically via scripts or malware routines that periodically send gathered files out without manual operator action.

T1020.001.description: Abuse native traffic mirroring on network devices or cloud services (AWS, GCP, Azure vTap) to duplicate and forward victim traffic to attacker-controlled destinations.

T1021.description: Log into remotely accessible services such as SSH, RDP, VNC, telnet or ARD using valid credentials to execute actions as that user and move laterally.

T1021.001.description: Use valid credentials to open interactive Remote Desktop Protocol sessions on remote Windows systems for lateral movement and hands-on GUI control.

T1021.002.description: Uses valid credentials or NTLM hashes to access Windows hidden admin shares over SMB for lateral file transfer and remote execution via RPC, services, scheduled tasks or WMI.

T1021.003.description: Remotely activates COM objects over RPC (DCOM) with admin credentials to execute commands, shellcode, Office macros or DDE on another host for lateral movement.

T1021.004.description: Logs into remote Linux, macOS or ESXi hosts over Secure Shell using valid passwords or keypairs, including enabling SSH on ESXi, to run commands as that user.

T1021.005.description: Remotely controls a machine's desktop via VNC screen-sharing over the RFB protocol, relaying screen, keyboard and mouse to act as the logged-on user.

T1021.006.description: Uses valid credentials over Windows Remote Management (WS-Management, ports 5985/5986) to run commands, modify registry or services on remote Windows hosts, often via PowerShell remoting.

T1021.007.description: Logs into cloud control planes or services via web console or CLI using on-premises synchronized/federated accounts or tokens to manage or access cloud resources.

T1021.008.description: Connects interactively to cloud VMs through provider-native console access like Azure Serial Console, EC2 Instance Connect or SSM Session Manager, often gaining root/SYSTEM, rather than running scripts.

T1025.description: Searches and collects files of interest from removable media such as USB drives or optical discs connected to a compromised system before exfiltration.

T1027.description: Encrypts, encodes, compresses, splits or otherwise obfuscates payloads, strings or commands on disk or in transit to hinder detection and analysis.

T1027.001.description: Appends or inserts junk data into a binary to change its hash and inflate file size beyond scanner or upload limits, evading signatures without altering functionality.

T1027.002.description: Compress, encrypt, or virtualize an executable with a packer or VM-based protector so its file signature changes and the original code is only unpacked or interpreted at runtime.

T1027.003.description: Hide code or data inside the bytes of digital media such as images, audio, or video, e.g., PowerShell embedded in PNG pixels via Invoke-PSImage, to evade detection.

T1027.004.description: Deliver payloads as uncompiled source code or non-native formats that are compiled on the victim with native or bundled compilers like csc.exe, ilasm.exe, or GCC before execution.

T1027.005.description: Modify a detected or quarantined tool to strip the specific signature or indicator that triggered detection, then reuse the altered version against the same or other targets.

T1027.006.description: Embed encoded payloads in HTML files as JavaScript Blobs or Data URLs that are reassembled and dropped on the victim browser, bypassing web and email content filters.

T1027.007.description: Hide imported API functions by storing hashes or encrypted names and resolving them at runtime via GetProcAddress/LoadLibrary or PEB walking, leaving no readable imports in the binary.

T1027.008.description: Remove symbols, strings, and other human-readable information from executables or scripts, such as stripped Go/ELF binaries or run-only AppleScripts, to hinder reverse engineering.

T1027.009.description: Conceal payloads inside otherwise benign files, such as binary overlays, resources, or nested same-format files, without steganographic weaving, often for later extraction or process injection.

T1027.010.description: Obfuscate command lines and scripts using escape characters, string splitting, encoding, casing tricks, environment variable substitution, or path traversal so commands evade signatures while still executing.

T1027.011.description: Store payloads or staged data in non-file locations like registry values, event logs, WMI repository, or RAM-backed directories such as /dev/shm to evade disk-based scanning.

T1027.012.description: Embeds payload download URLs in the icon location field (IconEnvironmentDataBlock) of Windows shortcut files so invoking the LNK fetches payloads past content filters, often executed via target-path arguments.

T1027.013.description: Encrypts or encodes whole files or specific values (C2 addresses, configs, payloads) using keys, Base64, BOM tricks, or password-protected documents and SFX archives to defeat static signatures until runtime decoding.

T1027.014.description: Uses polymorphic or metamorphic code that mutates into a functionally identical but differently structured version on each execution, defeating signature-based antivirus detection.

T1027.015.description: Compresses payloads or shellcode into archives such as ZIP, 7z, RAR, concatenated multi-directory ZIPs, or self-extracting archives to hide content from scanners and email filters.

T1027.016.description: Inserts non-executing or functionally irrelevant instructions, such as NOP (0x90) opcodes, into malware to obstruct disassembly and static analysis, unlike binary padding which only alters signatures.

T1027.017.description: Hides JavaScript inside XML-based SVG image files that assembles or downloads payloads, redirects to malicious sites, or renders fake login forms, evading filters that treat SVGs as benign images.

T1027.018.description: Conceals encoded payloads or prompt injections using non-rendering Unicode code points like zero-width spaces, variation selectors, bidi controls, or PUA characters, reconstructed at runtime via eval or JavaScript Proxy traps.

T1029.description: Schedules data exfiltration to occur only at specific times of day or fixed intervals to blend with normal traffic patterns, typically combined with another exfiltration channel.

T1030.description: Exfiltrates data in fixed-size chunks or packets kept below thresholds instead of whole files, avoiding network data transfer volume alerts.

T1033.description: Identifies the primary, currently logged-in, or frequent users of a system using commands like whoami, who, w, quser, dscl, environment variables, or network-device show users to shape follow-on actions.

T1036.description: Manipulates names, locations, metadata or appearance of artifacts so files, tasks, services or utilities look legitimate to users and security tools, evading detection and observation.

T1036.001.description: Copies code signing metadata and signature blocks from signed binaries onto unsigned payloads, producing invalid signatures that appear legitimate, unlike Code Signing which yields a valid signature.

T1036.002.description: Inserts the Unicode right-to-left override character U+202E into file names or registry keys so the displayed extension is reversed, disguising executables like .scr or .js as documents or images.

T1036.003.description: Renames or relocates legitimate system utilities and tools such as rundll32 or PsExec before execution to bypass detections keyed on their expected names or standard paths.

T1036.004.description: Names scheduled tasks, Windows services or systemd units, and their descriptions or display names, to mimic or duplicate legitimate benign ones and blend in with normal system entries.

T1036.005.description: Names or places files, registry keys, or container resources to match or approximate legitimate ones, such as svchost.exe in an unexpected directory or pods in trusted Kubernetes namespaces.

T1036.006.description: Appends a trailing space to a file name on macOS so a benign-looking extension like .txt is ignored and the OS determines and executes the true file type, such as a Mach-O binary.

T1036.007.description: Uses filenames with two extensions like File.txt.exe so hidden-extension views show only the benign first extension while the true executable extension determines execution, often in phishing attachments.

T1036.008.description: Alters a payload's header magic bytes, extension, icon or contents, or builds polyglot files, so malware appears as a benign file type and bypasses file validation during transfer or storage.

T1036.009.description: Breaks parent-child process lineage on Linux by double-forking or calling daemon() so the payload is reparented to init (PID 1), evading process tree-based detection.

T1036.010.description: Create or rename accounts with names mimicking legitimate service, backup, or generic accounts (admin, help, root) so they appear benign, distinct from impersonating specific people or organizations.

T1036.011.description: Overwrite a Linux process's in-memory argv strings with null bytes and write a spoofed argv[0] so /proc/PID/cmdline and ps display a benign command, without needing elevated privileges.

T1036.012.description: Spoof browser and system attributes such as User-Agent string, OS, language, platform, resolution, and time zone in web traffic to mimic a victim's profile and evade fingerprint-based detection.

T1037.description: Abuse scripts automatically executed at system boot or user logon to maintain persistence, potentially gaining elevated privileges when those scripts run under higher-privileged contexts.

T1037.001.description: Set the HKCU\Environment\UserInitMprLogonScript registry value to a script path so Windows runs it whenever the user logs on, providing per-user persistence.

T1037.002.description: Add a LoginHook or LogoutHook key to macOS com.apple.loginwindow.plist (via defaults) pointing to a script that runs as root at user login or logout; deprecated since macOS 10.11.

T1037.003.description: Assign logon scripts through Active Directory user attributes or Group Policy Objects so they execute at logon across many domain systems, achieving network-wide persistence.

T1037.004.description: Append binary paths or shell commands to Unix RC startup scripts such as rc.local or rc.common, which execute as root at boot; notably used on ESXi via /etc/rc.local.d/local.sh.

T1037.005.description: Create a directory with an executable and StartupParameters.plist in macOS /Library/StartupItems so the deprecated startup items mechanism runs it as root during the final boot phase.

T1039.description: Search and collect files of interest from accessible network shares and file servers on remote systems, staging sensitive data from shared drives prior to exfiltration.

T1040.description: Capture network traffic via promiscuous-mode interfaces, SPAN ports, cloud traffic mirroring or device capture commands to harvest cleartext credentials and environment details passively.

T1041.description: Exfiltrate stolen data by encoding it into the existing command and control channel, using the same protocol and destination as normal C2 communications.

T1046.description: Enumerate services listening on remote hosts and network devices via port, vulnerability or wordlist scans, or mDNS/Bonjour queries, to identify exploitable targets.

T1047.description: Abuse Windows Management Instrumentation locally or remotely over DCOM/WinRM to execute commands, spawn processes and query system information via wmic, PowerShell CIM cmdlets or COM APIs.

T1048.description: Exfiltrate data over a protocol or destination different from the main C2 channel, such as FTP, SMTP, DNS, SMB, HTTP or cloud platform downloads.

T1048.001.description: Exfiltrate data over a non-C2 protocol using manually implemented symmetric encryption like RC4 or AES with shared keys, layered on or inside otherwise plaintext protocols.

T1048.002.description: Exfiltrate data over a non-C2 protocol with built-in asymmetric/public-key encryption such as HTTPS, TLS or SSL, relying on the protocol's native encryption.

T1048.003.description: Exfiltrate data over unencrypted non-C2 protocols like HTTP, FTP or DNS, optionally obfuscating it with encoding, compression or embedding in protocol headers without encryption.

T1049.description: List active network connections to or from the compromised or remote systems, including sessions and cloud VPC links, using netstat, net session, lsof or device CLI commands.

T1052.description: Exfiltrate data by copying it to removable physical media such as USB drives, external disks or phones, often to bridge air-gapped networks.

T1052.001.description: Exfiltrate data by copying it to a USB-connected device, often to bridge air-gapped networks or hop between disconnected systems, rather than over a network channel.

T1053.description: Abuse OS task scheduling utilities to run code at startup, on a schedule, remotely, or under a privileged account for execution, persistence, and privilege escalation.

T1053.002.description: Schedule code execution with the legacy at utility on Windows, Linux, or macOS, including via the Win32_ScheduledJob WMI class, for persistence, remote execution, shell escapes, or sudo privilege escalation.

T1053.003.description: Add entries to crontab files so the Unix cron daemon runs malicious commands at startup or on time-based schedules, including on ESXi hosts via /var/spool/cron/crontabs/root.

T1053.005.description: Create Windows Task Scheduler tasks via schtasks, GUI, .NET, netapi32, or WMI for persistence, remote execution, or SYSTEM context, optionally hiding them by deleting the SD registry value.

T1053.006.description: Create systemd .timer unit files paired with .service files to run code on calendar or relative schedules, at root or user level, as a cron alternative on Linux.

T1053.007.description: Use Kubernetes CronJobs or Jobs to schedule deployment of containers running malicious code across cluster nodes, maintaining persistence through orchestrator-managed recurring tasks.

T1055.description: Execute arbitrary code within the address space of another live process to masquerade as legitimate execution, evade process-based defenses, and inherit its privileges and resources.

T1055.001.description: Inject a DLL into a remote process by writing its path and calling LoadLibrary via a remote thread, or via reflective loading or module stomping that overwrites a legitimate DLL's entry point.

T1055.002.description: Copy a full PE image directly into a target process's memory, fixing relocations, and execute it via a remote thread or shellcode, without loading a DLL from disk.

T1055.003.description: Suspends a thread in an existing live process, writes code into its memory, and redirects its instruction pointer via SetThreadContext before resuming; unlike hollowing, no new suspended process is created.

T1055.004.description: Queues malicious code or a LoadLibrary call onto a target thread's asynchronous procedure call queue via QueueUserAPC, executing when the thread becomes alertable; includes Early Bird and AtomBombing variants.

T1055.005.description: Manipulates thread local storage callback pointers in a PE's memory so the process runs injected code before reaching its legitimate entry point, typically combined with hollowing-style memory writes.

T1055.008.description: Attaches to a running Linux process with the ptrace syscall, writes code into its memory via PTRACE_POKETEXT/POKEDATA, and sets registers with PTRACE_SETREGS to redirect execution.

T1055.009.description: Enumerates a Linux process's memory mappings through /proc/[pid]/maps and overwrites its stack via /proc/[pid]/mem using dd with a ROP payload, bypassing ASLR without ptrace.

T1055.011.description: Writes payload to shared memory sections of a GUI process and places a pointer in a window class's Extra Window Memory via SetWindowLong, triggering it as a window procedure without WriteProcessMemory.

T1055.012.description: Creates a legitimate process in a suspended state, unmaps its image with NtUnmapViewOfSection, writes malicious code in its place, resets the thread context, and resumes it.

T1055.013.description: Overwrites a legitimate executable inside a TxF transaction, maps it into a section, rolls back the file change, then creates a process from the tainted section, avoiding hollowing APIs and on-disk artifacts.

T1055.014.description: Hijacks syscall stubs mapped from the Linux vdso shared object to open and map a malicious shared object, then redirects execution by patching the process's global offset table entries.

T1055.015.description: Copies a payload into a process hosting a SysListView32 list-view control, often via LVM_SETITEMPOSITION window messages, then triggers it as a sort callback by sending LVM_SORTITEMS.

T1056.description: Capture user input such as typed credentials via transparent interception or deceptive prompts and portals; parent technique covering keylogging, GUI prompts, web portal capture and credential API hooking.

T1056.001.description: Record user keystrokes via keyboard API hooks, raw hardware buffer reads, registry changes or custom drivers to harvest typed credentials over time, distinct from hooking credential-specific APIs.

T1056.002.description: Display spoofed OS or application authentication dialogs via AppleScript, PowerShell or shell scripts, imitating installers, UAC or browser prompts to trick users into entering credentials.

T1056.003.description: Modify externally facing login portals such as VPN or OWA pages to log and exfiltrate credentials submitted by users, either post-compromise for persistence or during initial exploitation.

T1056.004.description: Hook Windows APIs via hook procedures, IAT patching or inline hooks, or Linux/macOS functions via LD_PRELOAD and DYLD_INSERT_LIBRARIES, to capture parameters containing user credentials.

T1057.description: Enumerate running processes using tasklist, Get-Process, CreateToolhelp32Snapshot, ps, /proc, esxcli or network device show processes to understand installed software and shape follow-on actions.

T1059.description: Execute commands, scripts or binaries through built-in or cross-platform interpreters such as shells, PowerShell, Python, JavaScript or VBScript; parent technique for interpreter-based execution.

T1059.001.description: Execute PowerShell cmdlets and scripts, including download cradles, encoded commands and in-memory payloads, or invoke System.Management.Automation via .NET without powershell.exe.

T1059.002.description: Execute AppleScript via osascript, shebang scripts, NSAppleScript/OSAScript APIs, Mail rules or Automator to send AppleEvents, control applications, show fake dialogs or call native macOS APIs.

T1059.003.description: Execute commands and batch scripts through cmd.exe, either single commands via cmd /c, .bat/.cmd files, or interactive shells forwarded over a C2 channel or remote service.

T1059.004.description: Executes commands or shell scripts via Unix shells (sh, bash, zsh, Busybox) on Linux, macOS, or ESXi, interactively over C2/SSH or as scripted payloads for persistence.

T1059.005.description: Executes Visual Basic, VBScript, or VBA macro code, typically via wscript/cscript, HTA pages, or Office documents with embedded macros delivered in phishing attachments.

T1059.006.description: Executes Python commands or .py scripts via the interpreter, or Python-compiled executables, using built-in libraries to download, run commands, and perform host operations.

T1059.007.description: Executes JavaScript implementations: browser scripts, Node.js, Windows JScript via Windows Script Host/HTA, or macOS JXA via osascript/OSAKit, often obfuscated as secondary payloads.

T1059.008.description: Executes commands on network device CLIs (routers, switches) via console, telnet, or SSH to alter traffic flows, load malicious firmware via startup config, or disable logging.

T1059.009.description: Invokes cloud provider APIs through CLIs, browser Cloud Shells, PowerShell modules, or SDKs with stolen tokens to execute actions across tenant compute, storage, IAM, and networking.

T1059.010.description: Executes malicious code using AutoIT (.au3) or AutoHotKey (.ahk) Windows automation scripts, run by their interpreters or compiled into standalone executables, often delivered via phishing.

T1059.011.description: Executes Lua scripts through a standalone interpreter or Lua-embedded applications, including abusing or replacing existing embedded Lua interpreters to run malicious code at runtime.

T1059.012.description: Executes hypervisor management CLIs such as ESXi esxcli and vim-cmd to list, stop, or manipulate guest VMs and alter firewall or logging, often preceding VM encryption.

T1059.013.description: Executes commands via Docker CLI/API/SDK or Kubernetes API and kubectl to pull images, run containers, exec into pods, and enumerate cluster resources.

T1068.description: Exploit software, OS, or kernel vulnerabilities, including bringing a signed vulnerable driver (BYOVD), to elevate from user-level to SYSTEM/root or escape a VM or container to the host.

T1069.description: Enumerate groups and permission settings to learn which accounts exist, their group memberships, and which hold elevated privileges, across local, domain, or cloud scopes.

T1069.001.description: List local system groups and their members, such as the local Administrators group, using net localgroup, dscl on macOS, or groups on Linux.

T1069.002.description: Enumerate Active Directory or other domain-level groups and members, e.g., Domain Admins, via net group /domain, dscacheutil on macOS, or ldapsearch on Linux.

T1069.003.description: Enumerate cloud roles, groups, attached policies, and object ACLs using authenticated APIs like Get-MsolRole, Azure CLI, Google Cloud Identity API, or AWS IAM/S3 calls.

T1070.description: Selectively delete or modify host artifacts such as logs, command histories, or file metadata so intrusion activity blends with normal behavior and complicates timeline reconstruction.

T1070.003.description: Clear shell command history by running history -c, deleting .bash_history, removing PSReadLine ConsoleHost_history.txt, Clear-History, network device clear history, or editing ESXi shell.log.

T1070.004.description: Delete dropped malware, tools, and other intrusion files using del, rm, unlink, or secure-wipe utilities like SDelete to minimize on-disk footprint.

T1070.005.description: Remove mapped network share and SMB admin share connections after use, typically with net use \\system\share /delete, to erase lateral movement traces.

T1070.006.description: Alter file MAC timestamps, such as NTFS $SI or $FN attributes or via touch on Linux/ESXi, so new or modified files mimic legitimate neighbors and evade forensic review.

T1070.007.description: Delete or modify network connection artifacts such as RDP history registry keys, Default.rdp, bitmap cache, connection logs, or firewall/proxy configuration changes to hide remote access activity.

T1070.008.description: Delete emails, mailbox export requests, headers or mail logs via Exchange cmdlets, mail utilities, AppleScript or transport rules to erase evidence of phishing, collection, email C2 or exfiltration.

T1070.009.description: Remove previously established persistence artifacts such as services, scheduled tasks, Run keys, plists, executables or created accounts to erase evidence of an adversary's persistent presence.

T1070.010.description: Copy or move a delivered payload to new locations, often renaming it and deleting the original, to separate it from initial alerts, blend in, target exclusions or persistence paths.

T1071.description: Embed command and control traffic within standard OSI application layer protocols such as web, file transfer, mail, DNS or pub/sub to blend with legitimate network traffic.

T1071.001.description: Conduct command and control over HTTP/S or WebSocket, hiding commands and results in web request headers, cookies, URIs or bodies to mimic normal browsing traffic.

T1071.002.description: Conduct command and control over file transfer protocols like FTP, FTPS, TFTP or SMB, concealing commands in protocol fields or transferred files to blend with normal traffic.

T1071.003.description: Conduct command and control over mail protocols such as SMTP, POP3 or IMAP, hiding commands and results in email messages, headers or attachments exchanged with attacker mailboxes.

T1071.004.description: Conduct command and control over DNS, encoding commands and data in queries and records like TXT or A, often as low-frequency beaconing that blends into normal DNS resolution.

T1071.005.description: Conduct command and control over publish/subscribe protocols such as MQTT, XMPP, AMQP or STOMP, relaying commands through a centralized message broker via topics to mimic legitimate messaging.

T1072.description: Abuse centralized software deployment or configuration management suites to push and execute commands across many endpoints, enabling enterprise-wide lateral movement, collection, or destructive effects such as mass wiping.

T1074.description: Gather collected data into a central directory or instance before exfiltration, often combining files, to reduce C2 connections and evade detection.

T1074.001.description: Consolidate collected data in a directory, local database, or Windows Registry on the same compromised host prior to exfiltration.

T1074.002.description: Aggregate data collected from multiple compromised systems onto one central internal host or cloud instance before exfiltration, limiting outbound C2 connections.

T1078.description: Log in with credentials of existing legitimate accounts to gain access, persist, escalate privileges, or evade defenses without deploying malware.

T1078.001.description: Use built-in or vendor-preset accounts such as Windows Guest/Administrator, AWS root, ESXi vpxuser, or appliance factory credentials that were never changed.

T1078.002.description: Abuse credentials of Active Directory domain user, admin, or service accounts, often obtained via credential dumping or reuse, to access domain resources.

T1078.003.description: Abuse credentials of accounts configured on a single host or service, often reusing local admin passwords across machines for escalation and lateral movement.

T1078.004.description: Abuse cloud or SaaS user and service accounts, including federated or synced identities and managed identities, to access cloud resources and pivot to on-premises systems.

T1080.description: Plant or inject malicious code into files on shared network drives or repositories, such as infected binaries or masquerading LNK folders, so users opening them execute payloads remotely.

T1082.description: Gathers operating system version, patches, hotfixes, architecture and hardware details via systeminfo, uname, esxcli, network device CLI or cloud instance APIs to shape follow-on actions.

T1083.description: Enumerates files and directories on local hosts, network shares or network devices using shell utilities like dir, tree, ls, find, or native APIs to locate information of interest.

T1087.description: Enumerates valid accounts, usernames or email addresses on a system or environment via built-in commands, cloud interfaces or file searches to support brute-forcing, phishing or account takeover.

T1087.001.description: Lists local system user accounts and groups using net user, net localgroup, id, groups, /etc/passwd, dscl or esxcli, without querying a domain directory.

T1087.002.description: Lists Active Directory or other domain users and groups via net /domain commands, ldapsearch, dscacheutil or AD PowerShell cmdlets to identify privileged domain accounts.

T1087.003.description: Dumps email addresses and accounts from Exchange global address lists or Google Workspace directory using authenticated sessions, such as the Get-GlobalAddressList cmdlet or MailSniper.

T1087.004.description: Lists cloud and SaaS identity accounts, roles and service accounts with authenticated tools like aws iam list-users, az ad user list, Get-MsolRoleMember or gcloud iam commands.

T1090.description: Routes command and control traffic through intermediary proxies, port redirectors or CDNs to avoid direct connections to adversary infrastructure, possibly chaining multiple hops to hide the source.

T1090.001.description: Relays C2 traffic between compromised systems inside the victim network, often over SMB or peer-to-peer protocols, so only one internal host communicates externally.

T1090.002.description: Places Internet-facing proxies such as VPSs, cloud hosts or compromised external servers between victims and the C2 server, forwarding traffic to mask the true C2 destination.

T1090.003.description: Chains traffic through multiple proxies such as Tor, ORB networks of compromised routers, IoT devices and VPS, or P2P nodes so defenders cannot trace past the last hop to the true source.

T1090.004.description: Hides the true HTTPS destination by placing a benign domain in the TLS SNI field and the real C2 domain in the HTTP Host header, relying on shared CDN routing.

T1091.description: Spreads malware onto systems, including air-gapped ones, by copying or modifying files on USB and removable media and abusing Autorun or user execution when the media is inserted.

T1092.description: Performs command and control with disconnected or air-gapped hosts by relaying commands and files via removable media between them and an Internet-connected compromised system.

T1095.description: Communicates with C2 or between infected hosts using non-application-layer protocols such as ICMP, raw UDP/TCP, SOCKS, or ESXi VMCI sockets that evade application-level monitoring.

T1098.description: Modifies existing accounts, such as credentials, group membership, or permissions, to preserve or elevate access, including subverting policies like repeated password resets to extend credential lifetime.

T1098.001.description: Adds attacker-controlled credentials, such as service principal secrets or certificates, AWS access keys, login profiles, SSH key pairs, federation tokens, or app passwords, to cloud accounts for persistent access.

T1098.002.description: Grants extra mailbox or folder delegate permissions in Exchange, Office 365, or Google Workspace, including Default/Anonymous folder roles, so attacker-controlled accounts retain access to target mail.

T1098.003.description: Adds roles or IAM permissions to attacker-controlled cloud accounts, such as attaching AWS IAM policies or assigning Office 365 Global Administrator, including to external accounts, for persistent tenant access.

T1098.004.description: Appends attacker public keys to SSH authorized_keys files on Linux, macOS, ESXi, cloud VMs via metadata APIs, or network devices to enable persistent key-based SSH login.

T1098.005.description: Register an adversary-controlled device with an MFA system or Entra ID/Intune to bypass MFA and conditional access and keep persistent access to a compromised account.

T1098.006.description: Bind additional Kubernetes Roles or ClusterRoles, or modify ABAC policies, to an adversary-controlled user or service account to persist in a container orchestration cluster.

T1098.007.description: Add a controlled account to privileged local or domain groups such as Administrators, Remote Desktop Users, VPN, or sudo, using net localgroup, net group, or usermod, for persistent elevated access.

T1102.description: Relay C2 traffic through legitimate external web services like Google, Microsoft, or social media to blend with normal TLS traffic and shield back-end infrastructure.

T1102.001.description: Post encoded C2 domains or IP addresses on legitimate web services that malware retrieves to resolve and redirect to the actual C2 infrastructure.

T1102.002.description: Send commands and receive their output through the same legitimate web service, e.g., posting results as comments, documents, pull requests, or messages.

T1102.003.description: Retrieve commands from a legitimate web service without returning output over it, sending results via a different channel or not at all.

T1104.description: Use separate C2 stages with distinct infrastructure, where a first-stage callback profiles the host and delivers a fuller-featured second-stage RAT with its own server.

T1105.description: Download tools or files from external systems into the victim environment via C2, native utilities like certutil, curl, wget, package managers, or synced cloud storage.

T1106.description: Invoke native OS APIs or direct syscalls, such as CreateProcess, NtCreateProcess, or fork, to execute behaviors, often bypassing user-mode API hooks used by security sensors.

T1110.description: Systematically guess account passwords online against authentication services or offline against obtained hashes, using repetitive iterative attempts to gain account access; parent of guessing, cracking, spraying and stuffing.

T1110.001.description: Guess many passwords against a single account via login services like SSH, RDP, SMB, LDAP or Office 365 without prior credential knowledge, often causing lockouts and repeated logon failures.

T1110.002.description: Recover plaintext passwords offline from stolen password hashes using dictionary, brute-force or rainbow table attacks on adversary-controlled systems, outside the target network.

T1110.003.description: Try one or a few common passwords across many accounts to avoid lockouts, often throttled and using LDAP or Kerberos authentication to evade 4625 logon-failure alerting.

T1110.004.description: Replay username and password pairs from public breach dumps of unrelated services against target logins, exploiting password reuse across personal and business accounts.

T1111.description: Intercept MFA factors such as smart card PINs, hardware token codes via keylogging, or SMS/email one-time codes, including compromising SMS providers, to authenticate as the victim.

T1112.description: Create, change or delete Windows Registry keys and values locally or remotely to hide payloads, weaken defenses, enable execution, or conceal null-prefixed pseudo-hidden keys.

T1113.description: Capture images of the user's desktop using RAT features, native utilities or APIs like CopyFromScreen, BitBlt, xwd or macOS screencapture to gather on-screen information.

T1114.description: Collect or forward user email from mail servers or clients to obtain sensitive data or monitor incident response communications.

T1114.001.description: Copy locally stored email data, such as Outlook .pst and .ost files from user profile directories, directly from a compromised endpoint.

T1114.002.description: Access email remotely on Exchange, Office 365, or Google Workspace servers using stolen credentials or tokens, often searching mailboxes for keywords with tools like MailSniper rather than reading local mail files.

T1114.003.description: Create inbox or organization-wide transport rules that automatically forward victim email to attacker-controlled recipients, sometimes hidden via MAPI, maintaining persistent mail access even after credential resets.

T1115.description: Read data users copy to the system clipboard via APIs or utilities like Get-Clipboard, clip.exe, or pbpaste, optionally replacing contents such as cryptocurrency wallet addresses.

T1119.description: Automatically search for and gather internal data matching criteria such as file type, name, or location using scripts, built-in RAT functionality, or cloud APIs and ETL pipelines, often on intervals.

T1120.description: Enumerate attached peripheral devices such as USB drives, printers, cameras, keyboards, and smart card readers to understand the system environment or target further actions.

T1123.description: Record audio from microphones or voice and video call applications via OS or application APIs to eavesdrop on conversations, saving recordings for later exfiltration.

T1124.description: Query local or remote system time, time zone, or uptime using commands like net time, w32tm, or GetTickCount to schedule execution, infer victim locality, or trigger time bombs.

T1125.description: Capture video or periodic images from webcams or video call applications via device APIs, distinct from Screen Capture because it records camera input rather than the display.

T1127.description: Proxy execution of malicious code through signed developer, debugging, or build utilities so the trusted binary bypasses application control and Smart App Control reputation checks.

T1127.001.description: Embed C# or VB.NET inline tasks in an XML project file and run it with signed MSBuild.exe, which compiles and executes the code, bypassing application allowlisting.

T1127.002.description: Abuses ClickOnce .NET deployment (.application/.appref-ms) so payloads install without admin rights and run as children of dfsvc.exe, including via rundll32 dfshim.dll,ShOpenVerbApplication.

T1127.003.description: Executes malicious scripts through the JamPlus build utility via crafted .jam build files, leveraging the reputable developer tool to bypass application control such as Smart App Control.

T1129.description: Loads shared modules (DLLs, .so, .dylib) from arbitrary local or UNC paths via LoadLibrary or dlopen/dlsym to execute modular malware payloads within a process.

T1132.description: Encodes command and control traffic contents using binary-to-text or character encoding schemes to make C2 data harder to detect; parent of standard and non-standard encoding.

T1132.001.description: Encodes C2 traffic with standard, specification-compliant schemes like Base64, hex, MIME, or Unicode to obscure command and control content.

T1132.002.description: Encodes C2 traffic with custom or modified schemes diverging from protocol specifications, such as Base64 with a custom alphabet in HTTP request bodies.

T1133.description: Leverages external-facing remote services like VPNs, Citrix, exposed Docker/Kubernetes APIs, or Tor hidden services for initial access or persistent remote entry into a network.

T1134.description: Modifies or steals Windows access tokens to run under a different user or SYSTEM security context, bypassing access controls and elevating privileges.

T1134.001.description: Duplicates an existing user's token with DuplicateToken(Ex) and applies it to a thread via ImpersonateLoggedOnUser or SetThreadToken, rather than spawning a new process or creating a token.

T1134.002.description: Spawns a new process under another user's token using CreateProcessWithTokenW, CreateProcessAsUserW, or runas, often after duplicating or creating that token.

T1134.003.description: Create a new logon session and token from known credentials via LogonUser, then assign it to a thread with SetThreadToken; distinct from token theft because a fresh token is made rather than duplicated.

T1134.004.description: Spawn a process with an explicitly assigned parent PID via CreateProcess attributes to disguise parent-child relationships or inherit a SYSTEM parent's token for elevation.

T1134.005.description: Insert privileged or well-known SIDs into an account's Active Directory SID-History attribute so issued access tokens grant those identities' rights, enabling privilege escalation and cross-domain access.

T1135.description: Enumerate shared folders and drives on local or remote systems, e.g. via net view, net share or NetShareEnum, to locate data for collection and targets for lateral movement.

T1136.description: Create new local, domain or cloud accounts to establish secondary credentialed access for persistence without deploying remote access tools.

T1136.001.description: Create a local account on a single host, network device, ESXi server, firewall console or Kubernetes cluster using commands like net user /add, useradd or dscl for persistent access.

T1136.002.description: Create an Active Directory domain account, e.g. via net user /add /domain or New-ADUser, to retain persistent credentialed access across domain-joined systems.

T1136.003.description: Create cloud user or service accounts such as AWS IAM users, Azure service principals or GCP service accounts, often scoped narrowly, to maintain persistent tenant access.

T1137.description: Abuse Microsoft Office startup mechanisms such as template macros, add-ins, and Outlook rules, forms or Home Page so malicious code runs whenever an Office application launches.

T1137.001.description: Insert VBA macros into Office base templates like Word Normal.dotm or Excel PERSONAL.XLSB, or redirect template loading via GlobalDotName or search-order hijack, to execute code on application startup.

T1137.002.description: Creates the undocumented Office test\Special\Perf registry key pointing to an arbitrary DLL that loads every time an Office application such as Word or Excel starts.

T1137.003.description: Plants a malicious custom Outlook form in the user's mailbox that executes code when the adversary sends a specially crafted email invoking that same form.

T1137.004.description: Sets a legacy Outlook folder Home Page URL to a malicious HTML page that executes code whenever the configured folder is opened or reloaded in Outlook.

T1137.005.description: Creates a malicious Outlook mailbox rule that triggers code execution when the adversary sends an email matching the rule's crafted trigger conditions.

T1137.006.description: Installs malicious Office add-ins (WLL/XLL, VBA, COM, VSTO, Outlook add-ins) that execute code automatically each time the corresponding Office application launches.

T1140.description: Decodes, decrypts or reassembles obfuscated payloads on the host using malware routines or built-in utilities like certutil -decode or copy /b to recover executable content.

T1176.description: Installs or abuses extensions for browsers, IDEs or other host applications to gain persistence, inheriting the host application's permissions and blending into trusted extension ecosystems.

T1176.001.description: Installs malicious browser extensions via store, sideloading, Chromium Preferences/Secure Preferences tampering or macOS mobileconfig profiles to persist, steal credentials, run C2 or weaken browser security.

T1176.002.description: Installs or sideloads malicious extensions into IDEs like VS Code, IntelliJ or Eclipse, or abuses benign ones, so code runs each time the IDE launches.

T1185.description: Injects into a victim's browser process to inherit cookies, sessions and client certificates, proxying adversary traffic through it to access authenticated intranet resources and bypass 2FA.

T1187.description: Force a victim system to automatically authenticate to an attacker-controlled server via SMB, WebDAV or EFSRPC coercion, capturing NTLM hashes for cracking or relay using lure documents, LNK/SCF icons, or EfsRpcOpenFileRaw.

T1189.description: Compromise client endpoints when users browse to attacker-controlled or compromised websites that fingerprint browsers and plugins and deliver exploit code, distinct from exploiting internet-facing servers.

T1190.description: Exploit vulnerabilities or misconfigurations in internet-facing servers, services, databases, edge appliances or cloud-hosted applications to gain initial network access, as opposed to client-side browser exploitation.

T1195.description: Manipulate products, source code, development tools, update mechanisms or hardware before delivery to the final consumer so victims receive compromised software or devices through trusted channels.

T1195.001.description: Inject malicious code into third-party dependencies, package repositories, or CI/CD components like GitHub Actions, including typosquatted or re-registered abandoned packages, to compromise downstream consumers and builds.

T1195.002.description: Tamper with a vendor's application source code, build process, update/distribution mechanism, or compiled releases so legitimate software delivers a backdoor to customers.

T1195.003.description: Modify hardware components or firmware during manufacturing or distribution to embed hard-to-detect backdoors in servers, workstations, network gear or peripherals before customer receipt.

T1197.description: Abuse Windows Background Intelligent Transfer Service jobs via bitsadmin or PowerShell to download, execute, or exfiltrate files and persist through long-lived jobs with notification commands run on completion.

T1199.description: Leverage compromised third parties such as MSPs, contractors, or Microsoft partners with delegated admin rights to access victim networks or tenants through trusted, less-scrutinized connections.

T1200.description: Physically connect unauthorized hardware such as network implants, rogue wireless access points, keystroke injectors, or DMA devices to a system or network to gain access or intercept traffic.

T1201.description: Enumerates password complexity, length and lockout policy settings via OS commands, network device CLI or cloud APIs to tailor brute-force or password-spraying attempts that avoid lockouts.

T1202.description: Executes commands through alternate Windows utilities like forfiles, pcalua, WSL, Scriptrunner or ssh ProxyCommand instead of cmd.exe to bypass interpreter restrictions and evade detections.

T1203.description: Exploits vulnerabilities in client software such as browsers, Office, Adobe Reader or Flash to achieve arbitrary code execution, typically delivered via drive-by or phishing documents.

T1204.description: Relies on social engineering to make a user perform an action, such as opening a file, clicking a link, installing remote tools or running code, that triggers execution.

T1204.001.description: Relies on a user clicking a malicious link that leads to code execution, browser exploitation or download of a payload, typically following spearphishing link delivery.

T1204.002.description: Relies on a user opening a malicious file such as a document, LNK, ISO, SCR or executable, often masqueraded or password-protected, to execute code after spearphishing attachment delivery.

T1204.003.description: Relies on a user deploying a backdoored cloud machine image or container image from a public repository, causing malicious code like cryptominers to run in the instance.

T1204.004.description: Tricks users via fake errors or CAPTCHA prompts (ClickFix) into copying and pasting obfuscated commands into the Run dialog or terminal, bypassing download and email protections.

T1204.005.description: Relies on a user installing a malicious or typosquatted library from package managers like npm or PyPI or code repositories, executing embedded code at install or import.

T1205.description: Uses magic packets or packet sequences to trigger hidden functionality, such as opening closed ports, activating backdoors on listening services, modifying network device implants or waking systems via Wake-on-LAN.

T1205.001.description: Sends connection attempts to a predefined sequence of closed ports so a firewall or sniffing implant opens a hidden listening port or initiates a C2 connection.

T1205.002.description: Attaches BPF/libpcap filters to network sockets so a passive backdoor activates, such as spawning a reverse shell, only when a crafted packet matching the filter arrives.

T1207.description: Registers a fake domain controller via DCShadow, creating server and nTDSDSA objects, to replicate arbitrary Active Directory changes while bypassing normal event logging.

T1210.description: Exploits vulnerabilities in internal network services like SMB, RDP, MySQL, or vCenter to execute code on remote systems for lateral movement after initial compromise.

T1211.description: Exploits vulnerabilities in security tools, logging pipelines, or cloud/SaaS platforms to hide activity, suppress telemetry, or evade audit trails rather than directly disabling defenses.

T1212.description: Exploits software vulnerabilities in authentication mechanisms, such as Kerberos MS14-068 or cloud token signing flaws, or replays captured packets to obtain or forge credentials.

T1213.description: Mines collaboration, messaging, and database repositories such as Teams, Slack, CRM, or exposed cloud databases for documentation, credentials, PII, and network information.

T1213.001.description: Mines Atlassian Confluence wiki pages for development documentation, network diagrams, credentials, and internal resource links.

T1213.002.description: Mines SharePoint sites and document libraries for policies, network diagrams, technical documentation, credentials, and links to internal resources.

T1213.003.description: Collects proprietary source code and embedded secrets from private or internal code repositories like GitHub or GitLab after gaining access, distinct from public-repo reconnaissance.

T1213.004.description: Mine on-premises or cloud CRM platforms like Salesforce or Dynamics 365 for customer PII, purchase histories, and support interactions to enable phishing, SIM swapping, or downstream compromise.

T1213.005.description: Mine chat platforms such as Slack, Teams, or Google Chat for credentials, source code, internal links, proprietary data, and incident response discussions to exfiltrate or refine targeting.

T1213.006.description: Collect data from on-premises or cloud databases such as MySQL, MongoDB, or Snowflake, harvesting credentials, PII, and financial records for extortion, sale, or further operations.

T1216.description: Proxy execution of malicious files through trusted Microsoft-signed Windows scripts to bypass application control and signature validation, distinct from abusing signed binaries.

T1216.001.description: Abuse the signed PubPrn.vbs printer-publishing script with a script: parameter pointing to a remote .sct scriptlet to execute remote code, blocked on Windows 10+ by LDAP-only restriction.

T1216.002.description: Invoke the signed App-V script SyncAppvPublishingServer.vbs with an "n; command" argument to run PowerShell commands without directly launching powershell.exe, evading execution restrictions.

T1217.description: Enumerate browser bookmarks, history, and saved accounts from local browser files and databases to learn about users, internal resources, and additional targets.

T1218.description: Proxy execution of malicious content through signed or trusted native binaries, such as Microsoft-signed Windows utilities or Linux split, to bypass process and signature-based defenses.

T1218.001.description: Embed payloads in Compiled HTML Help (.chm) files rendered by hh.exe using Internet Explorer components, executing scripts or binaries and potentially bypassing application control.

T1218.002.description: Execute malicious Control Panel items (.cpl DLLs exporting CPlApplet) via control.exe, or register renamed DLLs under Control Panel\Cpls registry key to load on Control Panel launch.

T1218.003.description: Abuses the signed Connection Manager Profile Installer cmstp.exe with a malicious INF file to load DLLs or remote COM scriptlets, bypassing application control or UAC via auto-elevated COM interface.

T1218.004.description: Proxies execution of .NET code through signed InstallUtil.exe, which runs installer classes decorated with the RunInstaller(true) attribute, bypassing application control.

T1218.005.description: Executes HTA files or inline VBScript/JavaScript, locally or from URLs, via signed mshta.exe running outside Internet Explorer's security context to bypass application control and browser protections.

T1218.007.description: Abuses Windows Installer msiexec.exe to launch local or remote MSI packages or DLLs, evading application control and potentially running as SYSTEM when AlwaysInstallElevated is enabled.

T1218.008.description: Abuses the signed ODBC configuration utility odbcconf.exe, typically its REGSVR action or response files, to load and execute malicious DLLs while bypassing application control.

T1218.009.description: Proxies execution through signed .NET COM registration utilities Regsvcs or Regasm, which run code marked with ComRegisterFunction or ComUnregisterFunction attributes even when registration fails.

T1218.010.description: Abuses signed regsvr32.exe to load malicious DLLs or remote COM scriptlets via URL (Squiblydoo using scrobj.dll) without registry changes, bypassing application control.

T1218.011.description: Abuses signed rundll32.exe to load and run malicious DLL exports, ordinals, .cpl files or mshtml JavaScript, evading allowlists and obscuring code via W/A export-name tricks and masqueraded DLL names.

T1218.012.description: Abuses verclsid.exe, the shell extension verification host, with /S /C {CLSID} to instantiate malicious COM objects or remote scriptlets while bypassing application control.

T1218.013.description: Abuses signed App-V injector mavinject.exe to inject malicious DLLs into running processes via /INJECTRUNNING or add import descriptors via /HMODULE, masking injection under a legitimate binary.

T1218.014.description: Abuses signed mmc.exe to run malicious .msc console files or snap-ins, e.g. CLSID-linked COM payloads via mmc -Embedding or wbadmin.msc commands, proxying execution through Microsoft Management Console.

T1218.015.description: Abuses Electron/Chromium-based applications such as Teams, Slack or Chrome to spawn commands as child processes (e.g. --gpu-launcher) or run planted JavaScript inside the app's Node.js backend.

T1219.description: Uses legitimate remote access software, management tools, EDR response features or KVM hardware to establish an interactive command and control session with compromised hosts.

T1219.001.description: Abuses IDE remote development tunneling, such as VS Code 'code tunnel' or JetBrains, authenticated via GitHub accounts to obtain interactive C2 that blends with developer traffic and auto-reconnects.

T1219.002.description: Installs or abuses legitimate graphical desktop support and RMM software like TeamViewer, AnyDesk or ScreenConnect to remotely control victims' screens, keyboards and mice as a C2 channel.

T1219.003.description: Physically attaches IP-based KVM devices such as TinyPilot or PiKVM to target machines for hardware-level remote control that bypasses host software security; notably used by DPRK IT workers.

T1220.description: Executes JScript or VBScript embedded in local or remote XSL stylesheets via msxsl.exe or wmic /FORMAT (Squiblytwo) to bypass application control using trusted transform utilities.

T1221.description: Injects remote template references into OOXML document relationships or RTF \*\template control words so opening the document fetches a malicious payload or triggers SMB/HTTP forced authentication.

T1222.description: Modifies file, directory or symbolic link permissions, ownership and ACLs to access or tamper with protected files, often as a precursor to persistence, hijacking or ransomware encryption.

T1222.001.description: Alters Windows DACLs and file attributes using icacls, cacls, takeown, attrib or PowerShell Set-Acl to take ownership or grant access to protected files and folders.

T1222.002.description: Modifies Linux or macOS file and directory ownership, mode bits, or attributes using chmod, chown, or chattr to access protected files, lock out others, or enable persistence and hijacking.

T1480.description: Constrains payload execution to intended targets by checking for expected environment values such as domain, shares, devices, IPs, or user-agent, proceeding only on a match unlike sandbox evasion.

T1480.001.description: Derives a payload decryption key from target-specific environment values like domain, hostname, files, or IPs so the encrypted payload only decrypts and runs on the intended system.

T1480.002.description: Checks for or creates a unique system mutex or Linux lock file so malware runs only once per host, exiting if the mutex already exists to avoid reinfection.

T1482.description: Enumerates Active Directory domain and forest trust relationships via nltest, DSEnumerateDomainTrusts API, .NET, or LDAP to find lateral movement paths across domains.

T1484.description: Modifies domain or identity tenant configuration such as GPOs, domain trusts, or federation settings to escalate privileges or evade defenses across centrally managed environments.

T1484.001.description: Edits Active Directory Group Policy Objects in SYSVOL, e.g. ScheduledTasks.xml or GptTmpl.inf, to push tasks, disable tools, create accounts, or grant rights domain-wide.

T1484.002.description: Adds or alters domain trusts and federation settings, such as adding signing certificates, converting domains to federated, or registering new identity providers in Okta/AWS, to authenticate as any user.

T1485.description: Destroys or overwrites individual files on local, remote, or cloud resources, or deletes cloud objects, images, databases, and VMs, to make data irrecoverable rather than wiping disk structures.

T1485.001.description: Modifies cloud storage bucket lifecycle policies, e.g. via S3 PutBucketLifecycle, to automatically expire and delete all objects, used for extortion or erasing stored logs.

T1486.description: Encrypt files, disks, MBR, VMs or cloud storage objects and withhold the decryption key, typically ransomware demanding payment, often renaming files and spreading worm-like across networks.

T1489.description: Stop or disable services and processes to deny availability or unlock data stores like Exchange, SQL, or ESXi VMs before destruction or encryption, including disabling cloud service access.

T1490.description: Delete shadow copies, backup catalogs, snapshots and cloud backups or disable recovery features like WinRE and boot repair to prevent restoration after destructive or ransomware activity.

T1491.description: Modify visual content of internal or external systems to deliver messaging, intimidate, or claim credit, damaging integrity of the original content.

T1491.001.description: Deface internal systems by replacing desktop wallpapers, altering server login messages or internal websites to intimidate users, usually after other objectives are completed.

T1491.002.description: Deface externally facing websites or systems to push political messages or propaganda, discredit the organization, or set up follow-on drive-by compromise.

T1495.description: Overwrite or corrupt BIOS or device firmware flash memory so systems or hardware like motherboards, drives, or network devices become inoperable or unbootable.

T1496.description: Co-opt victim compute, bandwidth, messaging or other resources for adversary profit such as cryptomining, proxyware, SMS fraud or spam, degrading availability.

T1496.001.description: Use victim CPU/GPU compute in endpoints, servers, cloud or containers to mine cryptocurrency, often killing competing miners and causing system unresponsiveness.

T1496.002.description: Abuse victim network bandwidth and IP addresses by selling them to proxyware services, joining DDoS botnets, seeding torrents, or running internet-wide scanning.

T1496.003.description: Abuses a victim's web forms such as OTP or verification fields to send mass SMS to attacker-controlled premium numbers, earning telecom revenue share while inflating victim messaging costs.

T1496.004.description: Hijacks compromised SaaS or cloud services, enabling them if needed, to send mass spam/phishing email and SMS or proxy access to cloud-hosted AI models, incurring costs and exhausting quotas.

T1497.description: Detects virtual machine or sandbox analysis environments via artifacts, user activity, or timing and alters behavior, halts execution, or withholds payloads to evade analysis.

T1497.001.description: Inspects system properties such as registry keys, processes, services, MAC prefixes, CPU count, memory, disk size, hardware devices, and manufacturer strings for virtualization artifacts and exits if found.

T1497.002.description: Checks for genuine user activity such as mouse movements, clicks, browser history, or file counts, or waits for specific user interaction before activating to evade automated sandboxes.

T1497.003.description: Uses timing APIs, uptime, or clock measurements around sleep calls to detect sandboxes that accelerate or manipulate time, or delays execution to outlast analysis windows.

T1498.description: Exhausts network bandwidth to a target service with high-volume traffic, often distributed via botnets or spoofed sources, distinct from endpoint DoS that exhausts host resources.

T1498.001.description: Sends high volumes of packets directly from one or many systems, often a botnet, to saturate the target network using protocols like UDP, ICMP, or TCP.

T1498.002.description: Sends requests with the victim's spoofed source IP to third-party reflectors whose larger responses (DNS, NTP, memcached) amplify and redirect flood traffic at the target.

T1499.description: Degrades service availability by exhausting host system or application resources or forcing crashes across OS, server, or application layers without saturating the network bandwidth.

T1499.001.description: Floods an endpoint with TCP packets such as SYN or ACK to exhaust OS-imposed connection limits and state tables, denying service without consuming actual hardware resources.

T1499.002.description: Overwhelms specific network services like web or DNS servers with high-volume HTTP requests or repeated SSL/TLS renegotiations, exhausting the service software's resources rather than OS limits.

T1499.003.description: Repeatedly invokes resource-intensive features of an application, such as expensive web app functions, to exhaust system resources and deny access to the application or server.

T1499.004.description: Exploits software vulnerabilities to crash applications or systems, re-exploiting after automatic restarts to sustain a denial of service affecting dependent systems.

T1505.description: Installs malicious components into extensible server applications via legitimate developer extension features to establish persistent access.

T1505.001.description: Creates malicious SQL stored procedures, startup procedures, or CLR assemblies on database servers like MSSQL, often enabling xp_cmdshell, to persist and execute OS commands.

T1505.002.description: Registers a malicious .NET transport agent with Microsoft Exchange that processes mail in the transport pipeline, triggering adversary actions like attachment theft on specified email criteria.

T1505.003.description: Places a web script on an accessible web server that provides command execution or a CLI, using the server as a persistent gateway into the network.

T1505.004.description: Installs malicious ISAPI extensions, filters, or native/.NET IIS modules as DLLs to intercept and modify HTTP traffic, execute commands, or proxy C2 on IIS servers.

T1505.005.description: Patches or replaces termsrv.dll, or redirects the TermService ServiceDll registry value, to run payloads or enable features like concurrent RDP sessions for persistence.

T1505.006.description: Install malicious vSphere Installation Bundles on ESXi hypervisors, often forced or with forged XML descriptor acceptance levels, to persist across reboots by deploying backdoors, listeners and firewall rules at boot.

T1518.description: Enumerate installed software and versions on a host or cloud environment to identify vulnerable applications, deployment tools or targets and shape follow-on actions.

T1518.001.description: Enumerate installed antivirus, EDR, firewalls, sensors and cloud monitoring agents via process lists, registry, WMI or cloud APIs to decide evasion or whether to proceed.

T1518.002.description: Enumerate installed backup software and configurations such as Veeam or Acronis to prepare for destroying backups, inhibiting recovery or ransomware encryption.

T1525.description: Backdoor cloud VM or container images stored in the victim's own registry so newly provisioned instances using the latest image run implanted code, providing persistence.

T1526.description: Enumerate cloud services enabled in PaaS, IaaS or SaaS environments, including security and logging services, via provider APIs or tools like Pacu and Stormspotter.

T1528.description: Steal application access or refresh tokens, e.g. Kubernetes service account tokens, CI/CD API tokens, IMDS managed identity tokens or OAuth tokens via malicious consent apps, to access cloud APIs.

T1529.description: Shut down or reboot hosts, network devices or VMs via commands or APIs like ExitWindowsEx or NtRaiseHardError to disrupt availability, often after wiping or encryption.

T1530.description: Collect data directly from cloud object or SaaS storage like S3, Azure Blob or OneDrive via cloud APIs, often exploiting misconfigured public buckets or leaked credentials.

T1531.description: Delete, lock or change credentials and permissions of legitimate user accounts to deny access, often before ransomware encryption to hinder response and recovery.

T1534.description: Send phishing emails or chat messages from an already compromised internal account to colleagues, exploiting internal trust to spread payloads or harvest credentials within the same organization.

T1535.description: Create cloud instances or resources in unused or unmonitored geographic regions, or regions lacking advanced detection services, using compromised cloud admin accounts to operate undetected, often for cryptomining.

T1537.description: Exfiltrate data by sharing, syncing, or copying snapshots and backups to another adversary-controlled account on the same cloud provider, using native APIs and internal address space to avoid external transfer monitoring.

T1538.description: Use stolen credentials to browse a cloud provider's web dashboard GUI to enumerate services, resources, findings, and open ports without issuing manual API requests.

T1539.description: Steal web session cookies from browser disk storage, process memory, network traffic, injected JavaScript, or AiTM phishing proxies to later authenticate to web services without credentials or MFA.

T1542.description: Abuse firmware or boot-stage components that execute before the operating system loads, such as BIOS, UEFI, or boot drivers, to persist beneath host-based defenses.

T1542.001.description: Overwrite or flash malicious BIOS or UEFI/EFI system firmware on the motherboard to gain persistence that survives OS reinstallation and evades host defenses.

T1542.002.description: Install malicious firmware on hardware components like hard drives or peripherals, which have weaker integrity checks than system firmware, to run code outside the OS and survive disk re-imaging.

T1542.003.description: Modify boot sectors such as the MBR or VBR on BIOS systems, or files in the EFI system partition on UEFI systems, to execute malicious code before the operating system loads.

T1542.004.description: Replace the ROM Monitor boot loader firmware on Cisco network devices with an unauthorized image, locally or via TFTP, then reboot to gain stealthy persistent control of the device.

T1542.005.description: Reconfigure a network device to netboot an unauthorized, modified operating system image from an attacker-controlled TFTP server on startup or reset, persisting backdoors via standard boot functionality.

T1543.description: Create or modify OS-level background processes such as Windows services, systemd units, or macOS launch daemons/agents to execute payloads at boot or intervals, often gaining SYSTEM/root privileges.

T1543.001.description: Place or modify a .plist in a LaunchAgents folder with RunAtLoad or KeepAlive so the per-user launchd executes a payload at user login with user-level privileges.

T1543.002.description: Create or alter systemd .service unit files, ExecStart-style directives, User directive, symlinks, or generators so systemd runs payloads at boot or service start on Linux.

T1543.003.description: Install or modify Windows services or kernel drivers via sc.exe, registry Services keys, or CreateService APIs to run payloads as SYSTEM, including vulnerable driver loading and SDDL-hidden services.

T1543.004.description: Install or modify system-level plist files in /Library/LaunchDaemons so launchd runs a payload as root at boot before login, or hijack writable executables referenced by existing daemons.

T1543.005.description: Abuse container runtimes and node agents like Docker, Podman, or kubelet, e.g. restart=always containers or Kubernetes DaemonSets, to persist on hosts or escalate via rootful container access.

T1546.description: Register or modify OS or cloud event-driven mechanisms so that specific events like logons, application launches, or cloud actions trigger execution of payloads, often under privileged accounts.

T1546.001.description: Modify file-extension handler registry keys under HKEY_CLASSES_ROOT shell\open\command so opening a file of that type launches an attacker-specified command.

T1546.002.description: Set HKCU\Control Panel\Desktop screensaver registry values to point SCRNSAVE.exe at a malicious PE so it executes after a period of user inactivity.

T1546.003.description: Registers WMI event filters, consumers and bindings so code runs on events like logon, time or uptime, executed via WmiPrvSe.exe often as SYSTEM, optionally deployed via mofcomp-compiled MOF files.

T1546.004.description: Inserts commands into bash or zsh startup and logout configuration scripts so they execute whenever a user opens a login or interactive shell or a session ends.

T1546.005.description: Registers commands with the shell trap builtin so they execute when the shell or script receives specified interrupt signals such as ctrl+c or exit.

T1546.006.description: Modifies Mach-O binary headers to add an LC_LOAD_DYLIB command loading a malicious dylib on every launch, stripping LC_CODE_SIGNATURE to avoid signature check failures.

T1546.007.description: Registers a malicious helper DLL under HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Netsh so it loads and executes whenever netsh.exe runs, including when invoked by VPN or other software.

T1546.008.description: Replaces accessibility binaries like sethc.exe or utilman.exe with cmd.exe or a backdoor so key combinations at the logon or RDP screen spawn a SYSTEM shell without authentication.

T1546.009.description: Adds a DLL to the AppCertDLLs registry value under Session Manager so it loads into every process calling CreateProcess, CreateProcessAsUser or WinExec APIs.

T1546.010.description: Sets the AppInit_DLLs registry value so user32.dll loads a malicious DLL into nearly every process that loads user32.dll; disabled when Secure Boot is enabled.

T1546.011.description: Installs custom application compatibility shim databases (.sdb) via sdbinst.exe that hook targeted programs to inject DLLs, redirect executables, bypass UAC or disable protections whenever they run.

T1546.012.description: Sets IFEO Debugger or SilentProcessExit MonitorProcess registry values so a malicious program launches when a target executable starts or exits, also used to hijack accessibility tools or disable security software.

T1546.013.description: Modify PowerShell profile scripts (profile.ps1) so arbitrary commands run whenever a PowerShell session starts, enabling persistence and privilege escalation when higher-privileged accounts launch PowerShell.

T1546.014.description: Write plist rules to /etc/emond.d/rules/ so the macOS Event Monitor Daemon runs commands as root on events like startup or user authentication.

T1546.015.description: Replace registry references to COM objects (CLSID InprocServer32 or TypeLib entries) so legitimate component loading executes attacker DLLs or remote scripts instead, providing persistence.

T1546.016.description: Embed malicious pre- or post-install scripts in installer packages (macOS pkg, Debian maintainer scripts, Windows MSI) that execute with the installer's inherited elevated or root permissions.

T1546.017.description: Add or modify Linux udev rule files so a RUN+= action executes attacker content when matching hardware or device events occur, often detaching processes to escape systemd-udevd sandboxing.

T1546.018.description: Plant .pth files or sitecustomize.py/usercustomize.py modules in Python paths so arbitrary code executes automatically every time the Python interpreter initializes.

T1547.description: Configure OS autostart mechanisms such as registry entries, special directories, or kernel extensions so programs execute automatically at boot or logon for persistence or elevated privileges.

T1547.001.description: Add programs to Windows registry Run/RunOnce keys, BootExecute, or Startup folders so they execute automatically at user logon or system boot.

T1547.002.description: Register a malicious DLL in the LSA Authentication Packages registry value so lsass loads and executes it at system boot.

T1547.003.description: Register a malicious DLL as a Windows Time service time provider under W32Time\TimeProviders DllName so svchost loads it at startup as Local Service.

T1547.004.description: Modifies Winlogon registry subkeys (Notify, Userinit, Shell) so winlogon.exe loads attacker DLLs or executables at user logon, establishing persistence.

T1547.005.description: Registers a malicious Security Support Provider DLL in LSA Security Packages registry keys so lsass loads it at boot or via AddSecurityPackage, gaining access to plaintext credentials.

T1547.006.description: Loads malicious Linux loadable kernel modules or macOS kernel extensions to run code in Ring 0 at boot, often as rootkits hiding files, processes and network activity.

keywords: Reopen windows when logging back in
T1547.007.description: Adds a malicious application path to the macOS com.apple.loginwindow.[UUID].plist so the Reopen-windows feature relaunches it at user login.

T1547.008.description: Replaces or adds illegitimate drivers/DLLs loaded by the LSA subsystem so lsass.exe continuously executes the payload, providing persistence.

T1547.009.description: Creates or modifies .lnk shortcuts or symlinks, typically in the Startup folder or by changing an existing shortcut's target, so malware runs at boot or login.

T1547.010.description: Registers a malicious port monitor DLL via AddMonitor or the Print\Monitors registry Driver value so spoolsv.exe loads it as SYSTEM at boot.

T1547.012.description: Installs a malicious print processor DLL via AddPrintProcessor or the Print\Environments\...\Print Processors registry key so spoolsv.exe loads it with SYSTEM privileges.
