T1547.013.description: Adds or modifies XDG .desktop files in autostart directories with an Exec directive pointing to a malicious binary, executed when the Linux desktop environment loads at login.

T1547.014.description: Creates a key under Active Setup\Installed Components with a malicious StubPath value that Windows executes in the user's context at logon.

T1547.015.description: Adds macOS login items via AppleScript System Events or the Service Management Framework (SMLoginItemSetEnabled) so executables launch at user login, recorded in backgrounditems.btm.

T1548.description: Circumvents native OS privilege elevation controls such as UAC, sudo, setuid bits, macOS authorization prompts or cloud role mechanisms to gain higher-level permissions.

T1548.001.description: Sets or abuses setuid/setgid bits on Linux/macOS binaries so code runs with the file owner's or group's privileges, including hunting existing SUID binaries for shell escapes.

T1548.002.description: Bypasses Windows User Account Control to reach high integrity without a prompt, using auto-elevating binaries like eventvwr.exe, elevated COM objects, registry hijacks or injection into trusted processes.

T1548.003.description: Abuses sudo credential caching (timestamp_timeout, disabled tty_tickets) or sudoers entries like NOPASSWD to run commands as root on Linux/macOS without supplying a password.

T1548.004.description: Calls the deprecated macOS AuthorizationExecuteWithPrivileges API to prompt users for credentials and run code as root, with no check on the requesting program's origin or integrity.

T1548.005.description: Abuses cloud permissions for just-in-time role access, account impersonation, or passing roles to resources (AWS PassRole, GCP token creator, Exchange ApplicationImpersonation) to gain temporary elevated privileges.

T1548.006.description: Manipulates macOS TCC by editing or substituting TCC.db, or by abusing apps already granted permissions like Finder, to gain Full Disk Access, camera, microphone or screen access without prompts.

T1550.description: Authenticates using stolen alternate material such as password hashes, Kerberos tickets, access tokens or session cookies instead of plaintext passwords, bypassing access controls and MFA for lateral movement.

T1550.001.description: Uses stolen OAuth or cloud application access tokens to make authorized API requests to SaaS and cloud services without credentials, bypassing MFA and surviving password changes.

T1550.002.description: Authenticate as a user with a stolen NTLM password hash instead of the cleartext password, enabling lateral movement; overpass-the-hash additionally converts the hash into a Kerberos ticket.

T1550.003.description: Inject stolen or forged Kerberos TGTs or service tickets into a session to authenticate to remote systems without the account password, distinct from hash-based NTLM authentication.

T1550.004.description: Import stolen web session cookies into an adversary-controlled browser to access web or cloud applications as the victim, bypassing MFA because the session is already authenticated.

T1552.description: Search compromised systems for insecurely stored credentials in plaintext files, registry, shell history, private keys, metadata services or other artifacts rather than dumping them from OS memory.

T1552.001.description: Search local files and network shares for passwords in user-created files, configuration files, source code, cloud credential files or container logs.

T1552.002.description: Query the Windows Registry for stored passwords such as autologon credentials or application secrets, typically via reg query searches for password strings.

T1552.003.description: Read shell command history files such as .bash_history or PowerShell PSReadline ConsoleHost_history.txt to harvest credentials typed as command-line parameters.

T1552.004.description: Locate and steal private key and certificate files such as SSH keys, .pem or .pfx, Entra ID device keys, or network device keys for authentication or decryption.

T1552.005.description: Query the cloud instance metadata service at 169.254.169.254, directly or via SSRF, to retrieve IAM credentials, tokens and UserData secrets.

T1552.006.description: Retrieve Group Policy Preferences XML files from the domain controller SYSVOL share and decrypt embedded cpassword values using the publicly known AES key.

T1552.007.description: Query Docker or Kubernetes APIs, often via exposed daemons or pod service accounts, to retrieve credentials from container logs, cluster secrets, or API server stored authentication material.

T1552.008.description: Harvest passwords, API keys, or tokens shared in chat and collaboration services by accessing them live via endpoints, servers, admin portals, or abused integrations rather than stored log files.

T1553.description: Undermine OS or security-product trust mechanisms, such as signature checks, download attributes, or site warnings, so untrusted programs execute or connections proceed without user warnings or blocking.

T1553.001.description: Bypass macOS Gatekeeper by removing or avoiding the com.apple.quarantine xattr, or exploiting logic flaws in signing and notarization checks, so untrusted apps run without user prompts.

T1553.002.description: Sign malware with created, purchased, or stolen code-signing certificates to produce valid signatures that bypass signed-code execution policies, unlike invalid or forged signatures used for masquerading.

T1553.003.description: Hijack Windows SIP or trust provider DLL registry entries (Dll/FuncName) so WinVerifyTrust signature validation reports malicious code as validly signed, also enabling persistent execution in verifying processes.

T1553.004.description: Install a rogue trusted root CA certificate on a host so adversary-controlled TLS servers, intercepted traffic, or cloned-chain-signed code are trusted without browser or signature warnings.

T1553.005.description: Deliver payloads inside ISO, VHD, or archive containers so extracted or mounted files lack the Zone.Identifier ADS, evading SmartScreen and Office Protected View checks.

T1553.006.description: Modify code signing enforcement policies, such as enabling Windows test signing, disabling DSE via g_CiOptions kernel patching, or disabling macOS SIP, to permit unsigned or self-signed code execution.

T1554.description: Replace or patch legitimate host application binaries, like SSH clients, with backdoored code via entry point or IAT modification for persistence or credential capture, optionally blocking updates.

T1555.description: Search OS, application, password manager, or cloud vault credential storage locations to extract saved user passwords for reuse in lateral movement or restricted access.

T1555.001.description: Dump macOS Keychain credentials via the security command-line utility or by directly reading and decrypting login.keychain files using the user's login password.

T1555.002.description: Scan securityd daemon memory as root on macOS to recover the cached keychain master key and decrypt plaintext keychain passwords of logged-in users.

T1555.003.description: Extract saved website credentials from browser files such as Chrome Login Data or Firefox logins.json, decrypting via CryptUnprotectData or browser keys, or scraping browser process memory.

T1555.004.description: Enumerate or decrypt Windows Credential Manager vaults using vaultcmd, CredEnumerate APIs, reading .vcrd files with Policy.vpol keys, or keymgr.dll credential backups.

T1555.005.description: Steal credentials from third-party password managers such as KeePass by extracting the master password or unlocked plaintext entries from process memory, or brute forcing the database master password.

T1555.006.description: Request secrets directly from cloud-native secrets managers like AWS Secrets Manager, GCP Secret Manager, or Azure Key Vault using privileged cloud credentials or compromised services' API access.

T1556.description: Tamper with authentication components such as LSASS, SAM, PAM, or macOS authorization plugins to capture credentials or bypass authentication for persistent account access.

T1556.001.description: Patch LSASS in memory on a domain controller, e.g. Skeleton Key, injecting a master password that authenticates as any domain user until reboot.

T1556.002.description: Register a malicious password filter DLL under the LSA Notification Packages registry value so LSA passes plaintext passwords to it whenever accounts change passwords.

T1556.003.description: Patch or replace Linux/macOS Pluggable Authentication Module components like pam_unix.so to accept a hardcoded backdoor password or log plaintext credentials passed during authentication.

T1556.004.description: Implant code in a network device operating system image that checks for a hardcoded adversary password before passing other credentials to normal authentication, granting backdoor local access.

T1556.005.description: Enable Active Directory reversible password encryption on accounts via GPO, FGPP or Set-ADUser so newly set passwords can be decrypted to plaintext using userParameters values and LSA secrets.

T1556.006.description: Disable or tamper with multi-factor authentication for compromised accounts by excluding users from policies, registering attacker-controlled MFA methods, or breaking MFA server calls to force fail-open.

T1556.007.description: Backdoor hybrid identity authentication bridging on-prem AD and Entra ID, e.g. injecting DLLs into PTA agents or AD FS, or registering rogue PTA agents, to harvest credentials and authenticate as any user.

T1556.008.description: Register a malicious Windows network provider DLL in the registry so mpnotify.exe passes cleartext logon credentials to its NPLogonNotify function at every interactive logon.

T1556.009.description: Modify or disable identity provider conditional access policies or cloud IAM conditions, such as adding trusted IP ranges or removing MFA or region restrictions, to preserve access to compromised accounts.

T1557.description: Position an adversary-controlled system between networked devices by abusing traffic-steering protocols like DNS, ARP or LLMNR or downgrades, to intercept, sniff, modify or block communications and credentials.

T1557.001.description: Spoof responses to LLMNR, NBT-NS or mDNS name queries so victims authenticate to the attacker, capturing NTLM hashes for offline cracking or relaying them to SMB, LDAP, HTTP or MSSQL.

T1557.002.description: Send forged or gratuitous ARP replies mapping a target IP to the attacker's MAC address, poisoning local ARP caches to intercept or relay traffic on the network segment.

T1557.003.description: Spoof DHCP responses as a rogue server to push attacker-controlled DNS or gateway settings to clients, gaining an AiTM position, or flood DISCOVER messages to exhaust the address pool.

T1557.004.description: Host a fraudulent Wi-Fi access point mimicking a legitimate SSID or answering probe requests for known networks to lure clients, then sniff traffic or capture credentials via fake captive portals.

T1558.description: Steal or forge Kerberos TGT or service tickets from the KDC exchange to subvert domain authentication and enable Pass the Ticket access.

T1558.001.description: Forge Kerberos ticket-granting tickets using the KRBTGT account hash, allowing authentication as any Active Directory account and requesting service tickets from the KDC.

T1558.002.description: Forge Kerberos service (TGS) tickets with a target service account hash, granting access to a single service without contacting the KDC, which makes detection harder.

T1558.003.description: Request TGS service tickets for accounts with SPNs, or capture them from traffic, then crack the RC4-encrypted ticket portion offline to recover service account passwords.

T1558.004.description: Send AS-REQ messages for accounts lacking Kerberos preauthentication to obtain AS-REP data encrypted with the user's hash, then crack it offline for plaintext passwords.

T1558.005.description: Steal Kerberos tickets from Linux or macOS credential cache files or in-memory ccache entries to reuse them for Pass the Ticket, impersonation, or conversion to Windows format.

T1559.description: Abuse operating system IPC mechanisms such as pipes, sockets, COM, or DDE to execute arbitrary local code or commands through another process.

T1559.001.description: Invoke Windows COM objects and interfaces from scripts or binaries to execute code locally, create scheduled tasks, or perform fileless download and execution through COM server DLLs/EXEs.

T1559.002.description: Abuses Windows Dynamic Data Exchange to run commands via DDE fields in Office documents or formulas in CSV files, bypassing VBA macros, or invokes DDE remotely through DCOM.

T1559.003.description: Sends crafted messages to root-running macOS XPC service daemons or privileged helper tools, abusing weak client validation or input sanitization to execute code with elevated privileges.

T1560.description: Compresses and/or encrypts collected data before exfiltration to reduce size and hide contents, using utilities, third-party libraries, or custom methods.

T1560.001.description: Packages collected data with command-line archiving utilities such as 7-Zip, WinRAR, tar, zip, makecab, diantz, or certutil Base64 encoding before exfiltration.

T1560.002.description: Compresses or encrypts collected data in-process using linked or imported third-party libraries like zlib, libzip, or Python rarfile, rather than spawning an external archiving utility.

T1560.003.description: Compresses or encrypts collected data using malware-implemented routines such as XOR, custom stream ciphers, or reimplemented compression algorithms without external libraries or utilities.

T1561.description: Overwrites or corrupts raw disk data or structures via direct disk write access, or erases network device storage, to destroy system availability, often with worm-like spreading.

T1561.001.description: Overwrites arbitrary portions or all sectors of a storage device with random data via direct disk access or drivers like RawDisk, erasing disk sections rather than individual files.

T1561.002.description: Corrupts boot-critical disk structures like the master boot record or partition table, or formats network device file systems, rendering systems unable to boot.

T1563.description: Takes over existing remote service sessions such as SSH, RDP, or telnet to move laterally, hijacking established sessions instead of authenticating new ones with credentials.

T1563.001.description: Hijack an existing SSH session by abusing the SSH agent or its socket to reuse established public-key trust for lateral movement, rather than authenticating a new SSH session.

T1563.002.description: Steal another user's active or disconnected RDP session using tscon.exe with SYSTEM privileges, taking over the desktop without credentials or user prompts.

T1564.description: Abuse OS hiding features or isolated environments to conceal files, accounts, windows, data, or execution from users and security tools; parent of specific hiding methods.

T1564.001.description: Mark files or directories as hidden via attrib +h, leading-dot names, UF_HIDDEN/chflags, or whitespace-only names so they evade normal browsing and listings.

T1564.002.description: Hide created or modified user accounts from login screens and settings via macOS Hide500Users/dscl IsHidden, Windows SpecialAccounts UserList registry, or Linux display manager settings.

T1564.003.description: Run programs with invisible windows using scripting flags like -WindowStyle Hidden, registry WindowPosition offsets, plist UIElement, hidden desktops (hVNC), or LOLBins to conceal activity from users.

T1564.004.description: Store malicious data or executables in NTFS file attributes such as alternate data streams or extended attributes instead of normal file contents to evade scanning.

T1564.005.description: Implement a separate hidden or virtual file system in unused disk space, a dropped partition image file, or non-standard fragments to conceal malicious components and I/O.

T1564.006.description: Execute malicious code inside a virtual machine or sandbox (VirtualBox, QEMU, Windows Sandbox, rogue ESXi VMs) so host security tools cannot observe its activity.

T1564.007.description: Overwrite VBA source code in Office documents with benign or empty data while retaining malicious compiled p-code that executes when the Office version matches.

T1564.008.description: Create or modify mailbox inbox rules or organization-wide Exchange transport rules that delete, move, or mark-read emails matching keywords like phish or hack, hiding security alerts, C2, or replies from the victim.

T1564.009.description: Hide malicious code or executables inside a macOS file's deprecated resource fork, later extracting content at an offset to an executable location and running it, often encrypted until execution.

T1564.010.description: Overwrite command-line arguments in a Windows process's PEB after creation, spawning suspended with benign arguments then patching in malicious ones (or vice versa) to deceive process-creation logging and memory analysis.

T1564.011.description: Launch processes with nohup, PowerShell -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue, or similar so they ignore hangup and interrupt signals and survive logoff or C2 disconnect, without re-invocation persistence like Trap.

T1564.012.description: Drop payloads into folders or filenames already excluded from antivirus and file scanning, abusing existing default or well-known exclusions rather than adding new ones by tampering with security tool settings.

T1564.013.description: Bind-mount an empty or benign process's /proc directory over a malicious process's /proc/<pid> on Linux so ps, top and similar utilities display benign metadata, hiding the malicious process.

T1564.014.description: Embed a second-stage payload in a legitimate file's extended attributes on macOS or Linux via xattr or setfattr, later extracting, decoding and executing it while the file's hash and content stay unchanged.

T1565.description: Insert, delete, or alter data to influence business processes, decisions, or external outcomes, or hide activity, compromising data integrity rather than availability or confidentiality.

T1565.001.description: Modify data at rest such as databases, Office documents, stored emails, or custom file formats to influence outcomes or conceal activity, e.g. altering financial transaction records.

T1565.002.description: Intercept and alter data in transit over network connections or between system processes before it reaches storage or recipients, manipulating outcomes such as financial messages or hiding activity.

T1565.003.description: Modify application binaries or file associations so data is altered as it is accessed and displayed to users, deceiving business processes and decision making without changing stored data.

T1566.description: Send electronically delivered social engineering messages, targeted or mass, containing malicious attachments, links, or callback instructions to gain initial access to victim systems.

T1566.001.description: Email targeted victims a malicious file attachment such as Office document, PDF, archive, or disguised executable that runs or exploits a vulnerability when opened by the user.

T1566.002.description: Email targeted victims links to malware downloads, browser exploits, homograph or obfuscated URLs, OAuth consent grants, or device code authorization pages instead of attaching files.

T1566.003.description: Deliver spearphishing links or attachments through third-party services like social media, messaging apps, or personal webmail to bypass enterprise email controls after building rapport.

T1566.004.description: Use phone calls or voice communications to manipulate victims into visiting URLs, installing remote access tools, or approving MFA prompts, often impersonating trusted support staff.

T1567.description: Exfiltrate data to a legitimate external web service separate from the C2 channel, blending with normal TLS-encrypted traffic already permitted by firewalls.

T1567.001.description: Exfiltrate data to a code repository such as GitHub via its HTTPS API rather than over the primary C2 channel.

T1567.002.description: Exfiltrate data to cloud storage services like Dropbox, Google Drive, or MEGA, often using tools such as rclone, instead of the primary C2 channel.

T1567.003.description: Exfiltrate collected data by posting it to text storage sites such as Pastebin, distinct from API-based code repository exfiltration.

T1567.004.description: Exfiltrates data by posting it over HTTPS to webhook endpoints (Discord, Slack, webhook.site) or linking victim SaaS services to adversary webhooks for automated data pushes, blending with collaboration traffic.

T1568.description: Computes C2 parameters such as domain, IP address or port dynamically via an algorithm shared with adversary infrastructure, evading static blocklists and enabling fallback reconnection.

T1568.001.description: Hides C2 behind one domain whose A records (single-flux) or NS records (double-flux) rotate rapidly among many IPs using short TTLs and round robin, often via proxy botnet hosts.

T1568.002.description: Generates many pseudo-random or word-concatenated C2 domains, often time- or seed-based, so malware can locate rendezvous domains that defenders struggle to predict, block or sinkhole.

T1568.003.description: Performs arithmetic on IP addresses returned in DNS responses, such as using octets to derive the port, to determine the real C2 IP and port and bypass egress filtering.

T1569.description: Abuses operating system services or daemons, creating or interacting with them locally or remotely, to execute commands or programs, often for one-time execution rather than persistence.

T1569.001.description: Uses macOS launchctl subcommands like load, unload or start to execute programs as Launch Agents or Launch Daemons via the launchd service framework.

T1569.002.description: Executes payloads via the Windows Service Control Manager by creating, modifying or starting services with sc.exe, net or PsExec, locally or on remote hosts.

T1569.003.description: Uses Linux systemctl commands such as start or enable to execute programs as systemd services through the systemd init system and service manager.

T1570.description: Copies tools or files between already-compromised internal systems using SMB admin shares, RDP, scp, rsync, ftp or synced cloud folders, distinct from ingress transfer from outside.

T1571.description: Communicates using a protocol on a port not normally paired with it, or reconfigures victim services such as the RDP listening port via Registry, to bypass filtering and confuse traffic analysis.

T1572.description: Encapsulates one network protocol inside another, such as SSH port forwarding or DNS over HTTPS, to hide C2 traffic and route otherwise filtered traffic like RDP or SMB to unreachable systems.

T1573.description: Applies an encryption algorithm to command and control traffic itself instead of relying on protections inherent to the transport protocol, often with keys embedded in malware or configuration.

T1573.001.description: Encrypts command and control traffic with a known symmetric algorithm such as AES, RC4, DES, or Blowfish, using the same shared key for encryption and decryption.

T1573.002.description: Protects command and control traffic with public-key cryptography such as RSA or TLS, using asymmetric keys to encrypt data or exchange a session key.

T1574.description: Runs payloads by manipulating how the operating system locates and loads programs or libraries, poisoning directories, paths, or Registry locations for persistence, privilege escalation, or evasion.

T1574.001.description: Plants or substitutes malicious DLLs so a legitimate Windows program loads them via side-loading, search order hijacking, redirection, phantom missing-DLL names, or direct replacement, running code under a trusted process.

T1574.004.description: Places a malicious dylib with an expected name in a macOS @rpath search location or missing weak-linked dylib path so a legitimate application loads it at runtime.

T1574.005.description: Overwrites binaries used by installers or in insecure %TEMP% unpack subdirectories with weak write permissions so an elevated installer process executes the adversary's replacement binary.

T1574.006.description: Sets dynamic linker environment variables or files like LD_PRELOAD, /etc/ld.so.preload, or DYLD_INSERT_LIBRARIES so malicious shared libraries load first and hook functions in victim processes on Linux or macOS.

T1574.007.description: Places a malicious binary in a directory listed earlier in PATH, or modifies $PATH itself, so the OS resolves a commonly called program name to the attacker's executable.

T1574.008.description: Drops an executable named after a program invoked without a full path into the calling program's directory, or uses PATHEXT extension precedence like .com over .exe, so Windows launches it instead.

T1574.009.description: Exploits service or shortcut paths containing spaces without quotation marks by placing an executable in a higher-level directory, such as C:\program.exe, which Windows resolves first.

T1574.010.description: Overwrites a Windows service's executable or its directory contents due to weak file system permissions, so the replaced binary runs with the service's privileges, often SYSTEM, upon service start.

T1574.011.description: Abuses weak ACLs on service Registry keys to change ImagePath, FailureCommand, or add Performance/Parameters keys like AutodialDLL so service start loads attacker-controlled executables or DLLs.

T1574.012.description: Sets the COR_PROFILER environment variable (system, user, or process scope) so an unmanaged profiler DLL is loaded into every .NET process that loads the CLR.

T1574.013.description: Replaces a function pointer in a GUI process's PEB KernelCallbackTable, e.g. fnCOPYDATA, with a payload address, then triggers it via a Windows message to execute code.

T1574.014.description: Hijacks .NET assembly loading by tampering with .config files or environment variables, or creating custom application domains, so benign .NET applications load a malicious assembly.

T1578.description: Creates, deletes, or modifies cloud compute components such as instances, VMs, and snapshots to bypass access restrictions, evade detection, or remove evidence.

T1578.001.description: Creates a point-in-time snapshot of a cloud VM, disk, or volume, often mounting it on an attacker-created instance to access data bypassing restrictions on existing infrastructure.

T1578.002.description: Create a new cloud VM instance, often mounting snapshots of existing volumes under a looser security policy, to bypass firewall rules and permissions and operate without disturbing running instances.

T1578.003.description: Delete or terminate cloud instances after use to destroy forensic artifacts and evidence of activity, often instances the adversary previously created.

T1578.004.description: Revert a cloud instance to a prior state by restoring VM or storage snapshots, or by relying on ephemeral storage reset on restart, to erase evidence of activity.

T1578.005.description: Modify cloud compute settings such as service quotas, tenant-wide VM size policies, subscription associations or allowed regions to expand usable compute, e.g. for cryptojacking, without alerting the victim.

T1580.description: Enumerate IaaS resources like instances, snapshots, storage buckets and databases via cloud APIs or CLIs, focusing on service components rather than which cloud services exist.

T1583.description: Buy, lease, rent or freely obtain infrastructure such as servers, domains, botnets, proxies or web services to stage and run operations while hindering attribution.

T1583.001.description: Register or acquire domains, including typosquatted, homoglyph/IDN lookalike, expired reputable, or Route53-registered domains with private WHOIS, for phishing, drive-by delivery and C2.

T1583.002.description: Set up and operate adversary-controlled DNS servers to manage server-side DNS C2 traffic and provide conditional responses to malware, rather than hijacking existing DNS servers.

T1583.003.description: Rent virtual private servers from cloud providers, sometimes with minimal registration, to host operations such as C2 that are rapidly provisioned and hard to tie back to the operator.

T1583.004.description: Buy, lease or obtain physical or dedicated servers the adversary runs itself for phishing, watering holes or C2, instead of compromising third-party servers or renting VPSs.

T1583.005.description: Buy, lease, or rent an existing botnet or ORB network of compromised VPS, SOHO routers, or IoT devices, e.g. via booter/stresser services, for DDoS, phishing, or proxying C2.

T1583.006.description: Register accounts on legitimate web platforms like GitHub, Google, or Twitter to later host C2, exfiltration, or phishing content that blends into expected traffic.

T1583.007.description: Purchase and configure serverless functions such as Cloudflare Workers, AWS Lambda, or Apps Script to answer implants or proxy traffic to C2 from cloud-provider subdomains.

T1583.008.description: Purchase online search or display ads impersonating brands to lure victims to cloned sites with trojanized software, often cloaking ad clicks to hide malicious pages from ad-network crawlers.

T1584.description: Compromise third-party servers, domains, DNS, network devices, or web services rather than buying them, to stage operations and blend in with trusted, high-reputation infrastructure.

T1584.001.description: Hijack domains by taking over registrar accounts or exploit dangling DNS records for subdomain takeover, or shadow legitimate domains by adding malicious subdomains under them.

T1584.002.description: Compromise third-party DNS servers to alter records, redirecting traffic for credential harvesting, proving domain ownership to SaaS, or silently creating malicious subdomains.

T1584.003.description: Compromise VPSs owned by third parties to use as C2 or staging infrastructure, gaining the cloud provider's reputation while obscuring attribution.

T1584.004.description: Compromise third-party physical servers, including web servers for watering holes or mail servers for phishing, and repurpose them for staging or C2.

T1584.005.description: Build a botnet by compromising many third-party systems or take over an existing botnet by redirecting bots to adversary C2, then use it for DDoS or phishing.

T1584.006.description: Hijack legitimate users' accounts on third-party web services like GitHub, Twitter, Dropbox or SendGrid to use as C2, exfiltration or phishing infrastructure that blends into normal traffic and resists attribution.

T1584.007.description: Compromise existing serverless functions such as Cloudflare Workers, AWS Lambda or Google Apps Scripts to answer implants or proxy traffic to adversary C2 from trusted cloud-provider subdomains.

T1584.008.description: Compromise third-party network devices like SOHO routers and edge appliances, not for victim access but to host payloads, harvest credentials, inject content, or serve as proxy and botnet relays.

T1585.description: Create and cultivate new accounts and personas on social media, email, code hosting or cloud services to support social engineering, phishing, or free-trial infrastructure abuse.

T1585.001.description: Create fictitious or impersonating social media profiles, building history, photos and connections, to befriend targets and later deliver spearphishing via service.

T1585.002.description: Register new email accounts, often free or disposable, to send phishing, register domains and cloud trials, and anchor personas while avoiding attribution.

T1585.003.description: Register adversary-owned accounts with cloud providers like MEGA, Dropbox, OneDrive or AWS to host tools, receive exfiltrated data, or provision VPS and serverless infrastructure.

T1586.description: Take over existing third-party accounts via phished, purchased, brute-forced or insider-sold credentials, leveraging the established persona's trust instead of creating new accounts.

T1586.001.description: Hijack existing social media profiles through phishing, purchased or reused credentials to exploit their established connections and trust for reaching targets or spearphishing via service.

T1586.002.description: Take over legitimate email accounts to send trusted phishing or spam that evades reputation filters, hijack existing email threads, and register infrastructure.

T1586.003.description: Hijack existing third-party cloud accounts (storage, compute, messaging like SendGrid or SES) to host tools, exfiltrate data, send phishing, or abuse provider trust, rather than creating new accounts.

T1587.description: Build attack capabilities in-house or via exclusive contractors, such as malware, exploits, and self-signed certificates, instead of buying, downloading, or stealing them.

T1587.001.description: Write custom malware components such as payloads, droppers, backdoors, packers, and C2 protocols, sometimes embedding false-flag indicators to mislead attribution.

T1587.002.description: Generate self-signed code signing certificates to later sign executables or scripts, lending apparent authenticity without obtaining a certificate from a trusted CA.

T1587.003.description: Create self-signed SSL/TLS certificates for adversary infrastructure to encrypt C2 traffic or enable adversary-in-the-middle when installed as trusted roots.

T1587.004.description: Develop original exploits for software or hardware vulnerabilities, often discovered through fuzzing or patch analysis, rather than acquiring public or purchased exploits.

T1588.description: Acquire capabilities by purchasing, downloading, or stealing malware, tools, exploits, certificates, or vulnerability information from vendors, marketplaces, or other actors instead of developing them.

T1588.001.description: Buy, download, or steal existing malware such as payloads, backdoors, and packers, including via Malware-as-a-Service offerings or repurposing other actors' code.

T1588.002.description: Acquire legitimate or dual-use software tools like Cobalt Strike or PsExec via download, purchase, theft, or cracking, for post-compromise use or testing malware against AV/EDR.

T1588.003.description: Purchase code signing certificates via front companies or stolen identities, or steal signing keys from compromised third parties, to sign malicious code with trusted certificates.

T1588.004.description: Buy, steal, or freely obtain SSL/TLS certificates, including via front organizations or compromised certificate authorities, to encrypt C2 or enable adversary-in-the-middle on attacker infrastructure.

T1588.005.description: Acquire ready-made exploits by downloading public code, buying from exploit vendors or criminal marketplaces, or stealing them from other actors instead of developing them in-house.

T1588.006.description: Acquire vulnerability information by monitoring open or closed vulnerability databases and disclosures or compromising vulnerability researchers, to later find or build matching exploits.

T1588.007.description: Obtain access to generative AI tools like LLMs to automate reconnaissance, write phishing lures, generate or obfuscate scripts and payloads, and produce deepfake media for impersonation.

T1589.description: Collect victim identity details such as names, emails, credentials, and MFA configurations via phishing, authentication service probing, or exposed online data sets before targeting.

T1589.001.description: Gather victim account credentials pre-compromise from breach dumps, code repositories, dark web markets, infostealer log channels, cookie-harvesting watering holes, or compromised MFA/OTP providers.

T1589.002.description: Harvest target email addresses from public sources or enumerate valid ones by probing authentication endpoints such as Office 365 autodiscover and GetCredentialType.

T1589.003.description: Collect employee names from social media, company websites, or leaks to derive email address formats and craft believable phishing lures.

T1590.description: Gather victim network details such as IP ranges, domains, and topology via scanning, phishing, or open technical databases like WHOIS and passive DNS before targeting.

T1590.001.description: Gather victim domain properties such as owned domains, registrar, contacts, and name servers via WHOIS, DNS, or cloud endpoints like Office 365 GetUserRealm and autodiscover.

T1590.002.description: Collect victim DNS details such as name servers, subdomain, MX, TXT and SPF records, or attempt AXFR zone transfers, revealing hosts and third-party SaaS providers for targeting.

T1590.003.description: Identify second or third-party organizations and domains, such as MSPs or contractors, holding connected or elevated network access to the victim, enabling trusted relationship abuse.

T1590.004.description: Map the physical and logical arrangement of the victim's external and internal networks, including routers, gateways and other infrastructure devices, before intrusion.

T1590.005.description: Determine victim-owned public IP addresses and netblocks via WHOIS, passive DNS or scanning, deriving organization size, location, ISP and hosting details.

T1590.006.description: Discover the existence and specifics of victim firewalls, content filters, proxies, bastion hosts and network intrusion detection systems to plan evasion or capability development.

T1591.description: Gather details about the victim organization such as divisions, business operations and key employee roles from public sources or elicitation to support targeting.

T1591.001.description: Determine where the victim's offices, key resources and infrastructure are physically housed, also revealing legal jurisdiction, supporting physical access or hardware additions.

T1591.002.description: Identify victim partners, suppliers, contractors and supply chain or shipment paths to find third parties usable for supply chain compromise or trusted relationship access.

T1591.003.description: Learn the victim's operational hours, working days and timing of hardware or software purchases and shipments to time intrusions or supply chain interception.

T1591.004.description: Identify personnel identities and business roles within the victim organization, including key staff and their data access, to select targets for phishing.

T1592.description: Collect pre-compromise details about victim hosts such as names, IPs, OS and language via scanning, phishing, watering-hole profiling scripts, or User-Agent checks that serve malware only to target platforms.

T1592.001.description: Gather victim host hardware details such as device types, versions, and security components like card readers or encryption hardware from scans, phishing, job postings, or invoices before targeting.

T1592.002.description: Gather victim installed software and security product details, including versions extracted from banners, user agents, or metadata of victim-hosted PDFs and documents, to find vulnerable software or defenses pre-compromise.

T1592.003.description: Gather victim host firmware type and version details, mostly from public sources or phishing, to infer host configuration, age and patch level for exploitation or supply chain targeting.

T1592.004.description: Gather victim client configuration such as OS version, architecture, language, time zone, and virtualization via scanning, profiling scripts on compromised sites, phishing, or public data sets before targeting.

T1593.description: Search freely available websites and domains such as news, social media, hiring, and contract sites for victim information to support targeting, distinct from victim-owned sites or technical databases.

T1593.001.description: Search social media sites for victim organization announcements and staff roles, locations and interests, possibly creating fake profiles or groups to elicit further information.

T1593.002.description: Use search engines with specialized query operators like filetype or site to harvest victim information and locate leaked sensitive data such as credentials or network details.

T1593.003.description: Search public code repositories like GitHub or GitLab for victim information such as employee names, libraries, and accidentally leaked credentials or API keys, distinct from collecting from private internal repositories.

T1594.description: Browse or crawl victim-owned websites for employee names, contacts, locations and business relationships, including probing robots.txt, sitemap.xml, and hidden directories for sensitive content.

T1595.description: Probe victim infrastructure directly via network traffic to gather targeting information, distinguishing it from passive reconnaissance that involves no direct interaction with victim systems.

T1595.001.description: Scan victim-allocated public IP ranges, from simple ICMP pings to banner grabbing, to identify which addresses are live and what host software runs on them.

T1595.002.description: Scan targets for exploitable weaknesses by harvesting software versions from banners, listening ports, and network artifacts and matching them against known exploits or CVEs.

T1595.003.description: Iteratively brute-force or crawl web paths, directories, and cloud storage bucket names using generic or target-specific wordlists to discover hidden content and infrastructure rather than credentials.

T1596.description: Query freely available technical databases such as domain and certificate registrations, passive DNS, and Internet scan repositories to collect victim information without touching victim infrastructure.

T1596.001.description: Search DNS records or passive DNS repositories, or query nameservers and exploit misconfigurations, to map a target's subdomains, mail servers, nameservers, and internal hosts.

T1596.002.description: Query public WHOIS data held by regional Internet registries to obtain a victim domain's assigned IP blocks, registrant contact details, and DNS nameservers.

T1596.003.description: Search public digital certificate data and CT logs or inspect served SSL/TLS certificates to harvest victim organization names, locations, and associated domains.

T1596.004.description: Search content delivery network data and lookup tools to identify victim content servers and exploit CDN misconfigurations that expose sensitive files or unprotected portals.

T1596.005.description: Search public Internet scan databases that publish open ports, hostnames, certificates, and server banners to profile targets or find vulnerable hosts without scanning them directly.

T1597.description: Gather victim information from paid, private or non-public sources such as subscription databases, threat intel feeds, or dark web and cybercrime markets to support targeting.

T1597.001.description: Search private threat intelligence vendor feeds and portals for breach trends, targeted industries, and successful TTPs useful for targeting victims, distinct from actors monitoring reports about themselves.

T1597.002.description: Purchase technical victim data such as scan results, credentials, employee contacts, or infrastructure details from paid aggregation services or dark web markets to identify or exploit targets.

T1598.description: Send phishing messages via email, IM or other electronic means to trick targets into divulging credentials or sensitive data, rather than executing code as in T1566 Phishing.

T1598.001.description: Send spearphishing messages through social media, personal webmail or other non-enterprise services, often via fake recruiter personas, to build rapport and elicit credentials or environment details.

T1598.002.description: Email a spearphishing attachment that asks the recipient to fill in and return information or that renders a fake login portal (e.g., HTML smuggling) to harvest credentials.

T1598.003.description: Send spearphishing links to cloned or adversary-in-the-middle login pages, BitB popups, QR codes, or tracking pixels to capture credentials, session cookies, or victim profiling data.

T1598.004.description: Use phone calls, robocalls, or callback-phishing lures with spoofed numbers and impersonated support or partner personas to verbally elicit credentials or sensitive information.

T1599.description: Compromise perimeter or internal segmentation devices such as routers and firewalls and reconfigure their policy to pass normally prohibited traffic between trusted and untrusted networks.

T1599.001.description: Modify a boundary device's NAT configuration to route traffic between separated networks or rewrite packet addresses to obscure activity, sometimes via custom NAT in a patched device image.

T1600.description: Compromise a network device's encryption capability, e.g. via image modification, key-size reduction or disabling crypto hardware, so transmitted traffic can be decrypted, manipulated or collected.

T1600.001.description: Shrink the encryption key size or weaken cipher parameters on a compromised network device, often via injected CLI commands, so intercepted traffic becomes trivially decryptable without the key.

T1600.002.description: Disable a network device's dedicated encryption hardware, forcing software encryption on general processors that can then be weakened alongside key-space reduction.

T1601.description: Modify or replace the single-file monolithic operating system image of an embedded network device, in memory or storage, to weaken defenses or add adversary capabilities.

T1601.001.description: Patch a network device OS image in flash or live memory (via debug commands or implanted bootloader) to add implants, backdoors or falsified command output like fake version strings.

T1601.002.description: Install an older, weaker operating system version on a network device and set it to boot, regaining weaker ciphers and fewer defensive features.

T1602.description: Collect bulk administration data about managed devices from configuration repositories exposed through management protocols such as SNMP or Smart Install.

T1602.001.description: Query SNMP Management Information Base OIDs on managed devices to dump system details, routing tables, interfaces and running configuration for network mapping.

T1602.002.description: Retrieve network device running or startup configuration files via SNMP, Smart Install or management tools to harvest topology, software details and stored credentials.

T1606.description: Generate new web credentials such as cookies, tokens or SAML assertions using secrets or signing keys, rather than stealing existing ones, to access web or cloud services bypassing MFA.

T1606.001.description: Generate new web session cookies using stolen secrets, private keys or seed values to access web apps or SaaS services, differing from cookie theft because the cookies are freshly forged.

T1606.002.description: Forge SAML tokens with arbitrary claims and lifetimes using a stolen or adversary-created token-signing certificate or rogue federation trust, enabling SSO access as privileged accounts.

T1608.description: Upload, install or set up developed or obtained capabilities on acquired, compromised or web-service infrastructure before use in targeting operations.

T1608.001.description: Upload payloads or backdoored packages, images and binaries to adversary infrastructure, web services, IPFS, blockchain contracts or public repositories so victims or implants can retrieve them.

T1608.002.description: Place legitimate or dual-use tools such as PsExec on adversary-controlled servers, GitHub repos or PaaS so compromised hosts can download them, as distinct from uploading custom malware.

T1608.003.description: Install obtained or self-signed SSL/TLS certificates on adversary web or mail servers to encrypt C2 traffic or lend credibility to credential harvesting sites.

T1608.004.description: Stage exploit or profiling scripts on adversary or compromised websites, ads or writable cloud buckets so visiting browsers are compromised in later drive-by or watering hole attacks.

T1608.005.description: Set up HTML pages, cloned login portals, shortened or masked URLs and PaaS-hosted redirects that spearphishing links point to for credential harvesting or malware delivery.

T1608.006.description: Manipulate search engine or in-site search rankings via keyword stuffing, planted backlinks and cloaking to push malicious staged sites or repositories to victims searching for content.

T1609.description: Abuse container management services such as the Docker daemon, Kubernetes API server or kubelet to execute commands inside containers via exec calls or deployment entrypoints.

T1610.description: Deploys a new container via Docker create/start APIs, Kubernetes dashboard, or workloads like DaemonSets to run malicious images or payloads, or bypass network and user restrictions.

T1611.description: Breaks out of a container or VM to the underlying host via host filesystem bind mounts, privileged containers, mounted docker.sock, abused syscalls, or hypervisor and kernel exploits.

T1612.description: Builds a custom container image directly on the host through the Docker build API from a benign base image, embedding malware to evade registry-based malicious image detection.

T1613.description: Enumerates containers, images, pods, deployments, nodes and cluster status via Docker or Kubernetes APIs, dashboards, or container logs to plan lateral movement and execution.

T1614.description: Determines the victim host's geographic location via time zone, locale APIs, keyboard layout, cloud instance metadata availability zone, or external IP geolocation lookup services to gate further actions.

T1614.001.description: Checks system language via the Nls\Language registry key, language and keyboard layout APIs, or locale/$LANG, commonly to avoid infecting hosts in specific countries such as CIS states.

T1615.description: Enumerates Active Directory Group Policy settings and GPOs via gpresult, PowerView functions, or SYSVOL Policies share to find privilege escalation paths, security controls, and modifiable policies.

T1619.description: Enumerates objects within cloud storage buckets or containers using provider APIs like AWS ListObjectsV2 or Azure List Blobs, analogous to local file discovery for selecting data to retrieve.

T1620.description: Allocates and executes payloads directly in the current process's own memory, e.g. via Assembly.Load or memfd, avoiding disk-backed modules; differs from process injection by targeting itself.

T1621.description: Repeatedly triggers MFA push notifications, SMS, or calls using stolen credentials or SSPR until the fatigued user approves the request, bypassing multi-factor authentication.

T1622.description: Detects debuggers via API calls, PEB BeingDebugged flag, TracerPid, breakpoint, timing or SEH exception checks, then alters behavior, detaches, or floods debug output to avoid analysis.

T1647.description: Modifies macOS property list key-value pairs, such as LSUIElement, LSEnvironment or Dock entries, to hide app execution, inject environment variables, or enable persistence and defense evasion.

T1648.description: Abuses cloud serverless functions and automation workflows like Lambda, Power Automate or Apps Script to run arbitrary code, escalate via attached roles, or trigger persistent actions on cloud events.

T1649.description: Steals certificates from stores, registry or files, or requests/forges AD CS and Entra ID authentication certificates, abusing SAN/EKU misconfigurations or CA private keys to authenticate as accounts.

T1650.description: Purchases or obtains existing footholds in target networks from initial access brokers or partner groups instead of developing own initial access capabilities.

T1651.description: Abuses cloud management services such as AWS SSM Run Command, Azure RunCommand or Runbooks to execute scripts inside virtual machines through installed VM agents.

T1652.description: Enumerates local device drivers or kernel modules via driverquery, EnumDeviceDrivers, registry, lsmod or modinfo to identify host role, security tools, sandboxes, or vulnerable drivers.

T1653.description: Alters power settings via powercfg or similar to prevent sleep, hibernation, lock or shutdown, or deletes shutdown/reboot binaries, keeping infected machines running to preserve access.

T1654.description: Enumerates or exports system, security, cloud and SIEM logs using tools like wevtutil or CollectGuestLogs.exe to discover accounts, hosts and software or monitor incident response.

T1657.description: Steals money from victims through ransomware extortion, BEC fraud, unauthorized fund transfers, bank or cryptocurrency theft, for financial gain or to disguise destructive goals.

T1659.description: Inject malicious content into victim traffic via compromised upstream channels such as ISPs, either in-path or by racing fake responses, rather than hosting payloads on compromised websites.

T1665.description: Conceal C2 infrastructure by filtering or redirecting security tool and researcher traffic, geofencing, masking domains, using residential proxies or VPNs, and fronting with trusted services that conditionally redirect.

T1666.description: Alter IaaS resource hierarchies, such as leaving AWS Organizations, creating new accounts or subscriptions, or transferring Azure subscriptions to attacker tenants, to escape policies and logging.

T1667.description: Flood target inboxes with thousands of messages, often by auto-subscribing addresses to mailing lists, to bury alerts and set up follow-on fake help desk vishing.

T1668.description: Secure sole access to a compromised system by patching the exploited flaw, disabling vulnerable services, revoking privileges, or removing rival malware to block other threat actors.

T1669.description: Gain initial access by connecting to target Wi-Fi networks, physically nearby or via compromised dual-homed third-party systems in proximity, then sniffing or performing AiTM on the network.

T1671.description: Persist in SaaS environments by creating, adding, or hijacking OAuth application integrations whose consented access and tokens survive password resets, MFA, or disabling the consenting account.

T1673.description: Enumerate running virtual machines on a host or hypervisor, e.g. via esxcli, vim-cmd, or vCenter, typically ahead of stopping or encrypting VMs.

T1674.description: Simulate keystrokes via software or malicious HID devices to perform actions as the user, such as launching shells or pasting JavaScript into browser consoles.

T1675.description: Execute commands on ESXi-hosted guest VMs from the hypervisor by abusing VMware Tools daemon and vSphere guest operations APIs like StartProgramInGuest, without network access to the guest.

T1677.description: Inject malicious code into CI/CD builds by modifying pipeline config files, referenced scripts, or forked pull requests to steal pipeline secrets, run code on runners, or ship tainted artifacts.

T1678.description: Delay malware execution using sleep calls, scheduling, repeated benign commands like ping loops, or API hammering to outlast sandbox analysis windows and blend with benign activity.

T1679.description: Exclude specific files, extensions, directories, or system components from encryption or tampering so the system stays operational for ransom notes and avoids triggering alerts.

T1680.description: Enumerate local drives, disks, volumes and attributes like free space or serial number via OS commands, APIs, esxcli, or cloud CLIs, often before ransomware encryption.

T1681.description: Search open or closed threat intelligence about their own or peer campaigns to adapt operations, such as rotating published indicators or removing exposed domains, rather than researching victims.

T1682.description: Query publicly accessible AI services such as LLMs to aggregate and analyze open information on targets, personnel, technologies, and relationships for pretexts, phishing contacts, or coercion.

T1683.description: Create or generate non-code content such as text, audio, images, or video, manually or with AI, to build personas, impersonate entities, and support social engineering, fraud, or influence.

T1683.001.description: Author or AI-tailor written materials like phishing lures, decoy documents, fake job postings, credentials, and persona narratives, often translated or styled to mimic trusted senders.

T1683.002.description: Create or manipulate audio, images, and video, including deepfakes, cloned voices, fabricated profile photos and ID documents, or live altered calls, to impersonate individuals in operations.

T1684.description: Manipulate users through trusted business channels and pretexts like help desk, executive, or recruiter scenarios to obtain password or MFA resets, approvals, disclosures, or payload execution with minimal technical indicators.

T1684.001.description: Pose as a trusted executive, colleague, or vendor to persuade victims into sending money, divulging information, or taking actions, typically in BEC fraud using urgent payment-themed lures and lookalike domains.

T1684.002.description: Forge email headers such as FROM to appear as a legitimate sender, abusing weak or absent DMARC/SPF/DKIM enforcement or Microsoft 365 Direct Send to deliver unauthenticated spoofed mail.

T1685.description: Disable, degrade, or tamper with security tools and telemetry such as EDR, AV, Sysmon, ETW, or log forwarders by killing processes, stopping services, editing configs, or abusing drivers.

T1685.001.description: Disable the Windows EventLog service or alter audit policy via auditpol, secpol.msc, service config, or Autologger registry Start values so events stop being recorded, rather than clearing existing logs.

T1685.002.description: Disable or reconfigure cloud audit logging such as AWS CloudTrail/CloudWatch trails, multi-region logging, log validation, or M365 mailbox auditing and license downgrades to avoid recording activity.

T1685.003.description: Display falsified security tool interfaces or tray icons showing healthy or protected status after disabling defenses, concealing the loss of protection from users and defenders.

T1685.004.description: Disable or tamper with the Linux Audit system by stopping or killing auditd, editing audit.rules or audit.conf, or hooking libaudit functions so kernel-level audit events are not logged.

T1685.005.description: Clear existing Windows Security, System, or Application event logs using wevtutil cl, PowerShell Clear/Remove-EventLog, Event Viewer, or deleting .evtx files in winevt\Logs to erase intrusion evidence.

T1685.006.description: Delete or truncate Linux or macOS system logs under /var/log, such as auth, secure, wtmp/utmp, kernel, and cron logs, to remove evidence of intrusion activity.

T1686.description: Disable host or network firewalls or add/modify rules to permit blocked traffic, e.g., via netsh, iptables, or esxcli, including opening services like RDP on nonstandard ports.

T1686.001.description: Adds or modifies cloud security groups, ingress rules or firewall policies to permit any traffic to cloud instances, enabling access from untrusted IPs or control-plane-to-data-plane movement, e.g., for cryptomining.

T1686.002.description: Disables or alters ACLs, security zones or policy rules on routers, switches and perimeter firewalls to permit blocked traffic, opening internal subnets for C2 and lateral movement, often via exploited management interfaces.

T1686.003.description: Disables Windows Defender Firewall profiles or adds, deletes and modifies host firewall rules via netsh, PowerShell cmdlets, registry keys or Control Panel to open ports for remote services or C2.

T1687.description: Exploits programming flaws in security tools such as AV, EDR, firewalls or cloud/SaaS defenses to terminate, disable or bypass protections, distinct from configuration changes by using vulnerability exploitation.

T1688.description: Forces Windows to reboot into safe mode via BCD edits so EDR and third-party security services fail to start, optionally registering malware or COM objects under SafeBoot registry keys to run anyway.

T1689.description: Forces use of outdated, less secure versions of features via backward compatibility, such as PowerShell v2 lacking script block logging, HTTPS-to-HTTP stripping, or vulnerable boot managers bypassing Secure Boot.

T1690.description: Prevents shell command history recording by unsetting HISTFILE, zeroing history size, abusing HISTCONTROL ignorespace, redirecting or disabling PSReadLine history, or disabling logging on network device CLIs.
